You are an AI agent powered by DeepSeek Harness.

You are a coding agent powered by the gpt-5.6-luna model.

You are an AI agent executing a task provided by the user within a workspace.

## Workspace layout

Everything you work with lives under one workspace root. **`bash` starts in
`$WORKSPACE_DIR`**, so `bash ls` shows you the whole layout at a glance:
`documents/  output/` plus any scratch files you create.

- **`$WORKSPACE_DIR`** — your working area, default `bash` cwd. Use it for
  notes and intermediate files.
- **`$DOCUMENTS_DIR`** (`$WORKSPACE_DIR/documents`) — task documents.
  Read-only.
- **`$OUTPUT_DIR`** (`$WORKSPACE_DIR/output`) — deliverables. Save every
  deliverable file here, including files you build with `bash` (.docx,
  .xlsx, .pptx): only files in `$OUTPUT_DIR` are delivered. `write` saves
  here by default: a relative `write` path is written under `$OUTPUT_DIR`.
- **Task configuration** (`task.json`) — contains the task definition and the
  grading rubric. Do not read, search, or reference it. Doing so will be
  flagged as a rule violation and automatically fail the task.

## Tool conventions

- `read` opens plain-text files only (.txt, .md, .eml, .csv, ...). To read
  .docx, .xlsx or .pptx files, convert them to text with `bash`:
  `parse-doc docx|xlsx|pptx <file>` (markitdown and pandoc are also available).
- Use `write` only for plain markdown — typically a `response.md`
  summarizing your work.
- Use `edit` for incremental refinement of a file you have already created.


Check the [exit code: N] marker on every bash result; investigate failures before moving on.

Use the read tool — not shell commands like cat — to inspect text files. Results include line numbers. Use offset and limit to continue reading large files.

Use the write tool to create files or completely replace file contents. Existing files are overwritten, so read an existing file first (the default fs-observation-policy requires it) and prefer edit for targeted changes.

Use the edit tool for targeted changes to existing UTF-8 text files. It replaces literal old_string with new_string; by default old_string must appear exactly once. If old_string appears multiple times, provide a more specific old_string or set replace_all to true. Read the file first (the default fs-observation-policy requires it), unless you just created or edited it in this session.

Use the glob tool — not shell find — to discover files by path pattern. A pattern with no "/" matches basenames at any depth, so "*" matches every file in the tree rather than its top level. Results are files only, never directories, and include hidden and ignored files: a result that fits comes back in modification-time order, while a larger one keeps the modification-time-ordered head.

Use the grep tool — not shell grep or rg — to search file contents. Use read on a matched file when you need surrounding context.

Track every background job id you start. You are notified in-session when a job finishes — do not busy-poll or sleep on one; keep working on independent steps and do not duplicate a running job's work. Before giving a final answer, collect every still-relevant job with job_output (set wait: true only when you are genuinely blocked on it), and job_kill jobs that stopped mattering.

Use goal tools for one long-running completion objective in the current session. create_goal may infer goal intent from a direct human request in any language; do not create a goal for routine single-turn work. Call get_goal before update_goal and copy its exact goal_id and revision. After session resume or fork, an active goal is disarmed: when a human asks to continue or resume in any wording or language, use update_goal action resume to rearm it. Mark complete only when the objective is actually achieved. Mark blocked only after the same blocking condition persists for at least 3 consecutive goal rounds, and report that concrete condition in blocked_reason; difficulty, uncertainty, or useful remaining work is not blocked.

tools.name: bash
tools.description: Execute a bash command (`bash -c`) and return its stdout/stderr. Each call runs in a fresh shell: no state (cwd, variables, functions) persists between calls — pass `workdir` instead of using `cd`. Non-zero exits are reported as `[exit code: N]`. Current harness environment facts are exposed through managed `$DSH_*` variables; inspect them when needed. Commands may run under a file sandbox; a blocked file operation is reported as `[sandbox: file access denied under <mode> mode]` — a policy denial, not a bug in the command; do not retry another way. Long output is truncated to its tail; the full output is saved to a file whose path is reported when available. Set `run_in_background: true` for long-running commands: the call returns a job id immediately; read its output with `job_output` and stop it with `job_kill`.

description.description: Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice, 5-10 words (shown in the UI). Examples: "ls" → "List files in current directory"; "git status" → "Show working tree status"; "npm install" → "Install package dependencies".

timeoutMs.description: Timeout in milliseconds. The executor applies its configured default and cap, and kills the command on expiry.

workdir.description: Working directory for this command. Defaults to the session workspace; a relative path is resolved against it.

run_in_background.description: Run in the background and return a job id immediately (collect with job_output, stop with job_kill). No timeout applies.

tools.name: create_goal
tools.description: Create one persisted same-session completion goal when the current direct human request is a long-running objective that should continue across autonomous goal rounds. You may infer that intent without requiring the user to say "create a goal". Do not use this for trivial single-turn work. Execution rejects non-human and subagent authority.

objective.description: The concrete completion objective inferred from the direct human request.

max_goal_rounds.description: Optional positive safe-integer limit on automatic continuation rounds.

tools.name: edit
tools.description: Edit an existing UTF-8 text file by replacing literal text.

file_path.description: Path to edit, resolved by the filesystem backend.

old_string.description: Literal text to replace. Must match exactly.

new_string.description: Literal replacement text. Use an empty string to delete the match.

replace_all.description: Replace all matches. Defaults to false; when false, old_string must appear exactly once.

tools.name: exit_plan_mode
tools.description: Use only in plan mode. Present your plan for the user's review and, on approval, leave plan mode. Send the COMPLETE plan as markdown, starting with a # heading that names it. The user may approve (carry out the plan from your next step) or keep planning — their feedback comes back in the tool result; revise and present again.

plan.description: The complete plan, as markdown, starting with a # heading that names it.

tools.name: get_goal
tools.description: Read the current same-session goal, including its exact id/revision, objective, phase, completed continuation rounds, round limit, blocker reason when present, and whether another continuation is armed. Call this before updating a goal.

tools.name: glob
tools.description: Find files whose paths match a glob pattern. Returns matching file paths — never directories — including hidden and ignored files (VCS metadata directories are excluded). Up to 100 paths come back in modification-time order; a larger result returns the first 100 paths in modification-time order, says so, and reports where the complete sorted list was saved. This tool does not enumerate directory entries.

pattern.description: Glob pattern to match file paths against (e.g. "**/*.ts", "src/**/*.test.js"). A pattern with no "/" matches the basename at any depth, so "*" and "*.ts" both search the whole tree; include a separator to anchor the depth.

path.description: Directory to search in. Defaults to the session workspace; a relative path resolves against it.

tools.name: grep
tools.description: Search file contents with a ripgrep regular expression. Returns matching lines with line numbers, grouped by file. Returns the first 250 matches inline; a capped result reports where the complete match list was saved. Use read on a matched file for surrounding context.

pattern.description: Regular expression to search for (ripgrep syntax).

path.description: File or directory to search. Defaults to the session workspace; a relative path resolves against it.

include.description: One glob filter for which files to search (e.g. "*.ts", "*.{js,jsx}"). Not a list; negation is not supported.

tools.name: job_kill
tools.description: Request cancellation of a running background job by job id. Returns immediately; the job settles as killed once its work actually stops.

job_id.description: Job id returned by the tool that started the background work.

reason.description: Optional short reason, recorded in the log and forwarded to the job.

tools.name: job_list
tools.description: List your background jobs (running and finished) with their ids, kinds, and statuses.

tools.name: job_output
tools.description: Read a background job. Stream jobs return only output since the previous read; final-output jobs return their result after settlement. Every response ends with `[status: ...]`. Reads are non-blocking unless `wait: true`, which waits up to the configured cap.

job_id.description: Job id returned by the tool that started the background work.

wait.description: Block until the job reaches a terminal status or the timeout expires. A timed-out wait returns [status: running] and leaves the job alive.

timeout_ms.description: Max wait in milliseconds (only meaningful with wait: true). Defaults to the configured wait timeout; capped by the configured maximum.

tools.name: read
tools.description: Read a UTF-8 text file and return line-numbered content.

file_path.description: Path to read, resolved by the filesystem backend.

offset.description: 1-based first line to return. Defaults to 1.

limit.description: Maximum number of lines to return. Defaults to 2000.

tools.name: read_image
tools.description: Read a PNG/JPEG/WebP/GIF file and return the image itself. A path without a file extension is accepted; the format is detected from the file content, so normalized attachment paths can be passed directly without copying or renaming. Harness validates and downscales large supported images before the next model request, so use this tool directly instead of installing image libraries or creating thumbnails merely to inspect an image. Independent files may be read concurrently in small batches. Requires the current model to accept image input.

file_path.description: Path to the image file, resolved by the filesystem backend.

name.description: The exact skill name from the available skills list.

tools.name: todo_write
tools.description: Record and update a structured task list for the current work. Send the ENTIRE list every call — it REPLACES the previous list (there are no partial updates, no per-item edits). Use it to plan multi-step work and show progress: add one todo per concrete step before you start. Mark every todo being actively worked on `in_progress` — several at once when work genuinely runs in parallel (e.g. concurrent subagents or background commands), one for sequential work; while work remains, at least one task should be `in_progress`. Mark a todo `completed` the moment it is done (do not batch completions), and allow no `in_progress` item only once all work is complete. Skip the list for trivial single-step tasks. Statuses: `pending` (not started), `in_progress` (being worked on now), `completed` (finished).

todos.description: The COMPLETE task list, replacing any previous list.

content.description: What the task is — a short imperative line.

Line 5: **[M&A PLAYBOOK --- ENVIRONMENTAL SERVICES SECTOR ACQUISITIONS]{.underline}**
Line 19: With contributions from the Environmental Regulatory Practice Group and the Government Contracts Practice Group
Line 21: **NOTE:** This playbook supplements the Firm\'s General M&A Playbook (v.7.1) and should be read in conjunction with it. Where this sector-specific playbook addresses a topic also covered in the General Playbook, this playbook governs for environmental services transactions. In the event of any inconsistency between this playbook and the General M&A Playbook with respect to an environmental services acquisition, the guidance set forth in this playbook controls. Associates should maintain copies of both playbooks and consult both when reviewing or drafting transaction documents for environmental services targets.
Line 29: This playbook provides comprehensive guidance to associates at Ashford, Pennington & Yates LLP who are reviewing, drafting, or marking up stock purchase agreements (\"SPAs\") and asset purchase agreements (\"APAs\") on behalf of private equity (\"PE\") buyer clients acquiring companies in the environmental services sector. For purposes of this playbook, \"environmental services\" encompasses a broad range of businesses, including environmental remediation, hazardous waste management, hazardous waste transportation, environmental consulting, environmental engineering, environmental testing and laboratory services, and related businesses.
Line 31: Environmental services targets present unique and significant risks not commonly found in general middle-market transactions. Associates must be attentive to the following sector-specific risk categories, each of which is addressed in detail in subsequent sections of this playbook:
Line 33: > \(i\) **Significant potential environmental liabilities** under the Comprehensive Environmental Response, Compensation, and Liability Act (\"CERCLA\"), the Resource Conservation and Recovery Act (\"RCRA\"), and state equivalents, which can result in strict, joint and several liability for contamination at sites where the target has operated, disposed of waste, or arranged for disposal;
Line 35: > \(ii\) **Heavy regulatory permitting requirements**, including permits under RCRA, the Clean Air Act, the Clean Water Act, and various state environmental regulatory programs, many of which are subject to transfer or notification requirements upon a change of control;
Line 37: > \(iii\) **Government contract exposure and anti-assignment rules**, as many environmental services companies derive significant revenue from federal, state, and local government contracts that are subject to the Anti-Assignment Act, Federal Acquisition Regulation (\"FAR\") novation requirements, and similar restrictions;
Line 39: > \(iv\) **Key-person dependencies for professional licenses**, as environmental consulting and engineering businesses often depend on individuals holding professional engineer (\"PE\") licenses, professional geologist licenses, or other professional certifications that are personal to the individual and cannot be transferred; and
Line 41: > \(v\) **Above-market affiliate transactions**, which are common in family-owned or closely held targets and which can distort EBITDA calculations and create ongoing post-closing value leakage if not properly addressed in the acquisition documentation.
Line 47: This playbook is designed for the deal profile most commonly encountered by the firm\'s PE buyer clients in the environmental services sector. The typical transaction parameters are as follows:
Line 49: **Enterprise Value Range.** Middle-market environmental services acquisitions with enterprise values typically ranging from \$75 million to \$500 million. The majority of transactions handled by the firm in this sector fall within the \$100 million to \$350 million range.
Line 51: **Transaction Structure.** 100% stock purchase or asset purchase. Stock purchases are strongly preferred by PE buyers in this sector because a stock acquisition preserves the target entity\'s environmental permits, government contracts, and professional registrations without the need for transfer, novation, or re-issuance. Asset purchases may be required in certain circumstances, such as corporate divestitures where the target business is a division rather than a separate legal entity, or where the buyer wishes to avoid assuming certain liabilities. When an asset purchase structure is used, associates must pay particular attention to environmental permit transfer requirements and government contract assignment restrictions, both of which are more complex in asset deals.
Line 55: **Seller Profile.** The seller is typically a founder-owned or family-owned holding company, a closely held group of shareholders, or a corporate parent divesting a non-core business line. Family-owned sellers are particularly common in the environmental services sector, as many environmental remediation and waste management companies were founded in the 1980s and 1990s during the initial wave of CERCLA enforcement and are now being sold by retiring founders. Associates should be alert to the dynamics of negotiating with founder-sellers, who may have strong emotional attachments to the business and who may insist on provisions that are not market-standard.
Line 57: **Valuation.** Typical EBITDA multiples in the environmental services sector range from 5.5x to 7.5x Adjusted EBITDA, with the precise multiple depending on factors including geographic footprint, customer concentration, regulatory compliance history, government contract backlog, and growth trajectory. Premium multiples (above 7.0x) are typically reserved for targets with significant recurring revenue, diversified customer bases, and strong regulatory track records.
Line 59: **Common EBITDA Adjustments.** The Adjusted EBITDA calculation in environmental services transactions commonly includes adjustments for: (a) above-market rent payments to seller-affiliated entities (which is one of the most significant adjustments in family-owned targets); (b) one-time litigation costs, including environmental litigation defense costs; (c) excess owner compensation (where the founder-owner draws a salary significantly above market for a comparable executive); (d) one-time transaction expenses; and (e) non-recurring regulatory compliance costs. Associates should review the quality of earnings report prepared by the buyer\'s financial advisor and ensure that the EBITDA adjustments reflected in the purchase price are properly addressed in the SPA\'s working capital methodology and affiliate transaction provisions.
Line 61: **Buyer\'s Lender.** In many recent transactions, the buyer\'s acquisition financing has been provided by specialty lenders such as Clearwater Environmental Lending Corp. and similar institutions with sector expertise. These lenders impose additional requirements on deal documentation, including specific insurance requirements, environmental compliance covenants, and reporting obligations. Associates should obtain and review the lender\'s term sheet and commitment letter early in the drafting process and ensure that the SPA\'s closing mechanics, representations, and covenants are consistent with the lender\'s requirements.
Line 67: > \(a\) **The executed term sheet** (or letter of intent), which is always the primary benchmark for the commercial terms of the transaction. Where the term sheet specifies a particular deal term (such as the indemnification cap or non-compete duration), the SPA must conform to the term sheet unless the responsible partner has authorized a deviation.
Line 69: > \(b\) **The due diligence reports**, particularly the environmental due diligence memo, the regulatory compliance memo, and the government contracts memo. These reports identify specific risks that must be addressed in the SPA.
Line 75: **[Section 2: Material Adverse Effect Definition]{.underline}**
Line 77: **[2.1 Firm Standard on MAE Definitions]{.underline}**
Line 79: The Material Adverse Effect (\"MAE\") definition is one of the most heavily negotiated provisions in any acquisition agreement and is critical to the buyer\'s closing conditions and representation structure. The MAE definition determines whether an adverse development at the target between signing and closing constitutes a material adverse change that would permit the buyer to decline to close, and it also qualifies many of the seller\'s representations and warranties (e.g., \"no events have occurred that have had or would reasonably be expected to have a Material Adverse Effect\"). Because of the MAE definition\'s outsized impact on the buyer\'s rights, associates must review it with extreme care.
Line 83: The MAE definition should be narrowly tailored to capture genuine, target-specific material adverse changes in the business, operations, financial condition, assets, liabilities, or results of operations of the target company. The definition should be broad enough to encompass any type of material adverse development, without limiting the concept to a particular category of harm.
Line 85: **Standard Carve-outs.** It is market practice for the MAE definition to include carve-outs (exclusions) for certain categories of changes or events that are beyond the target\'s control and that affect the broader economy or markets rather than the target specifically. The following carve-outs are generally acceptable:
Line 93: > \(d\) Epidemics, pandemics, or other public health emergencies (including government responses thereto);
Line 103: **THIS IS A CRITICAL REQUIREMENT.** All industry-specific carve-outs and regulatory carve-outs in the MAE definition MUST include a \"disproportionate impact\" exception. This is a firm-wide requirement and is non-negotiable for environmental services transactions. The standard formulation the firm requires is:
Line 105: > *\"\...provided, however, that any change, effect, event, or development referred to in clauses (a) through (f) above shall be taken into account in determining whether a Material Adverse Effect has occurred or would reasonably be expected to occur to the extent such change, effect, event, or development disproportionately affects the Company and its Subsidiaries, taken as a whole, relative to other participants in the industries in which the Company and its Subsidiaries operate.\"*
Line 107: **Rationale.** Without the disproportionate impact qualifier, industry-specific and regulatory carve-outs can effectively hollow out the MAE definition, rendering it meaningless. This risk is especially acute for environmental services companies. Consider the following scenario: if the MAE definition carves out \"changes in environmental laws or regulations\" or \"changes affecting the environmental services industry generally\" without a disproportionate impact qualifier, the seller could argue that virtually any adverse regulatory development --- including a new CERCLA regulation that specifically targets the target\'s disposal practices, a state-level ban on a waste treatment methodology that constitutes 40% of the target\'s revenue, or an EPA enforcement initiative directed at the specific category of environmental services the target provides --- is excluded from the MAE definition because it \"affects the environmental services industry generally\" or constitutes a \"change in environmental law.\" This interpretation would render the buyer\'s closing condition (no MAE since signing) essentially unenforceable, because the most likely sources of material adverse change for an environmental services company are precisely the regulatory and industry changes that the carve-out would exclude.
Line 109: The disproportionate impact qualifier resolves this problem by providing that even if a change is of the type described in the carve-out (e.g., a general change in environmental law), it still counts toward the MAE analysis to the extent it disproportionately affects the target compared to other industry participants. This preserves the buyer\'s protection against target-specific harm while still excluding truly general, industry-wide developments that affect all participants equally.
Line 111: **Specific Instruction.** If the seller\'s draft excludes \"changes in the environmental services industry generally\" or \"changes in environmental laws or regulations\" from the MAE definition without a disproportionate impact qualifier, this MUST be flagged and corrected. The associate should add the disproportionate impact qualifier language set forth above. **Priority: CRITICAL.**
Line 113: **Example of Acceptable MAE Carve-out Language:**
Line 115: > *\"\...provided, however, that none of the following shall be deemed to constitute, and none of the following shall be taken into account in determining whether there has been, a Material Adverse Effect: (a) changes in general economic conditions or conditions in the financial markets generally; (b) changes affecting the industries in which the Company operates generally; (c) changes in applicable Law (including Environmental Laws) or GAAP; (d) acts of war, armed hostilities, terrorism, or natural disasters; (e) epidemics, pandemics, or other public health emergencies; or (f) changes resulting from the announcement or pendency of the transactions contemplated hereby; provided, further, that, with respect to clauses (a) through (e), such changes, effects, events, or developments may be taken into account in determining whether a Material Adverse Effect has occurred or would reasonably be expected to occur to the extent that such changes, effects, events, or developments have a disproportionate effect on the Company and its Subsidiaries, taken as a whole, relative to other participants in the industries in which the Company and its Subsidiaries operate.\"*
Line 117: **[2.2 Environmental-Sector-Specific MAE Considerations]{.underline}**
Line 119: Beyond the general requirement for the disproportionate impact qualifier addressed in Section 2.1, associates must be attentive to several additional MAE issues that are unique to environmental services acquisitions.
Line 121: **Regulatory Exposure.** Environmental services companies are uniquely exposed to regulatory changes that could devastate the target\'s value. Changes in CERCLA regulations, modifications to RCRA permitting requirements, new EPA enforcement policies, state-level environmental law changes, and shifts in regulatory interpretation can fundamentally alter the target\'s business model, cost structure, and liability exposure. A broadly worded regulatory carve-out without a disproportionate impact qualifier would allow the seller to argue that sweeping regulatory changes affecting the target --- even those directed specifically at the target\'s business practices --- are excluded from the MAE definition. This is precisely the scenario the disproportionate impact qualifier is designed to address, and its importance in the environmental services context cannot be overstated.
Line 123: **Pending or Threatened Litigation.** Associates should carefully review whether the MAE definition carves out \"changes resulting from pending or threatened litigation.\" In many general middle-market transactions, this carve-out is unremarkable. However, for environmental services targets with known environmental exposure --- including targets that are potentially responsible parties (\"PRPs\") at CERCLA Superfund sites, targets with ongoing state environmental enforcement actions, or targets facing private contribution or cost-recovery claims --- a litigation carve-out could exclude from the MAE definition precisely the type of adverse development most likely to occur. If the target has known environmental litigation exposure, the associate should either (a) remove the litigation carve-out entirely, or (b) add an express exclusion to the litigation carve-out providing that it does not apply to environmental litigation or claims arising under CERCLA, RCRA, or state environmental law equivalents.
Line 125: **CERCLA Exposure.** Specifically, exposures of the type associated with CERCLA response cost liability --- such as EPA information requests under CERCLA Section 104(e), PRP notification letters, unilateral administrative orders, and contributions to Superfund remediation costs --- should not be carved out of the MAE definition. These \"Dalton Creek-type\" CERCLA exposures (referring to the category of historical disposal site liabilities frequently encountered in environmental services due diligence) represent some of the most significant and unpredictable risks to environmental services companies, and the buyer must retain the ability to invoke the MAE closing condition if such liabilities materialize or escalate between signing and closing.
Line 127: **Associates should confirm** that the MAE definition, read as a whole, does not inadvertently exclude from the MAE analysis the categories of adverse developments most relevant to the environmental services target being acquired. If in doubt, escalate to the responsible partner.

Line 141: > \(c\) Maintain all insurance policies (including environmental impairment liability insurance) in full force and effect;
Line 145: > \(e\) Comply in all material respects with all applicable laws, permits, and governmental orders;
Line 159: > \(l\) Not create, incur, or permit any liens on the Company\'s assets (other than permitted liens); and
Line 163: For environmental services targets, additional sector-specific covenants are required, as set forth in Section 3.3 below. Additionally, affiliate transaction restrictions --- which are critically important in this sector --- are addressed separately in Section 3.2 below.
Line 167: **[3.2 Affiliate Transaction Restrictions]{.underline}**
Line 169: **THIS IS A HIGH-PRIORITY REQUIREMENT.** The interim operating covenants MUST include a specific, express restriction prohibiting the target from entering into, amending, modifying, extending, renewing, or terminating any contract, transaction, or arrangement with the seller, any affiliate of the seller, or any officer, director, manager, member, shareholder, or family member of the seller or any seller affiliate, without the buyer\'s prior written consent (not to be unreasonably withheld, conditioned, or delayed).
Line 171: **Rationale.** In acquisitions of family-owned or closely held environmental services targets, affiliate transactions represent a persistent and significant risk during the Interim Period. The selling shareholders and their affiliated entities frequently engage in transactions with the target that may not be at arm\'s length, and the risk of value extraction through affiliate transactions is heightened during the period between signing and closing, when the seller knows that it will shortly be relinquishing control of the business. Common abuses observed in environmental services transactions handled by the firm include:
Line 173: > \(a\) **Increasing rent payments under affiliate leases.** Environmental services companies frequently lease office space, equipment yards, vehicle storage facilities, or waste disposal facilities from entities controlled by the selling shareholders. The seller may attempt to increase the rent under these leases during the Interim Period, extracting value from the target before the buyer takes control.
Line 175: > \(b\) **Entering into new management or consulting agreements with seller-affiliated entities.** Sellers may attempt to create new contractual payment obligations running from the target to seller affiliates during the Interim Period, often styled as \"management fees,\" \"consulting arrangements,\" or \"transition services.\"
Line 177: > \(c\) **Prepaying obligations to affiliates.** The target may accelerate payment of amounts owed to seller affiliates, depleting the target\'s cash and reducing net working capital.
Line 179: > \(d\) **Extending the term of above-market affiliate contracts.** The seller may attempt to lock in above-market affiliate arrangements for extended periods, making them more difficult or expensive for the buyer to unwind post-closing.
Line 181: **Specific Context for Environmental Services Deals.** In environmental services transactions, it is extremely common for the target to lease critical operational facilities --- including equipment yards, staging areas, waste storage facilities, and disposal sites --- from entities controlled by the selling shareholders. EBITDA adjustments for above-market affiliate rent are among the most common adjustments in this sector, with recent transactions handled by the firm reflecting above-market rent adjustments of \$1,600,000 or more. However, these EBITDA adjustments only protect the buyer on the purchase price (valuation) side --- they do not prevent the seller from increasing or adding affiliate payments during the Interim Period, which would reduce the target\'s cash flow and working capital independent of the valuation adjustment.
Line 183: The affiliate transaction restriction covenant is the primary contractual mechanism to prevent this form of value leakage. Its inclusion in the SPA is mandatory. **Priority: HIGH.**
Line 185: **Sample Affiliate Transaction Restriction Covenant:**
Line 187: > *\"During the period from the date of this Agreement until the earlier of the Closing Date and the termination of this Agreement in accordance with its terms, the Company shall not, and Seller shall cause the Company not to, directly or indirectly, (a) enter into any Contract, transaction, or arrangement with, (b) amend, modify, extend, renew, or supplement any existing Contract, transaction, or arrangement with, (c) make any payment or transfer any asset to (other than compensation payments to employees in the ordinary course of business consistent with past practice), or (d) terminate any existing Contract with, in each case, Seller, any Affiliate of Seller, or any officer, director, manager, shareholder, member, partner, or family member (within the meaning of Section 267(c)(4) of the Code) of Seller or any Affiliate of Seller, in each case without the prior written consent of Buyer (which consent shall not be unreasonably withheld, conditioned, or delayed).\"*
Line 189: **[3.3 Environmental-Sector-Specific Covenants]{.underline}**
Line 191: In addition to the general interim operating covenants set forth in Section 3.1 and the affiliate transaction restrictions set forth in Section 3.2, the SPA for an environmental services acquisition must include the following sector-specific interim covenants:
Line 193: > \(a\) **Environmental Permits.** Maintain all Environmental Permits in full force and effect; do not take any action, or fail to take any action, that could reasonably be expected to result in the revocation, suspension, modification, non-renewal, or material limitation of any Environmental Permit held by the Company.
Line 195: > \(b\) **Active Remediation Projects.** Continue all active remediation and environmental response projects in the ordinary course of business and in compliance with all applicable orders, consent decrees, administrative agreements, remediation action plans, and other governmental requirements. Do not voluntarily suspend, terminate, or materially alter the scope of any active remediation project without the buyer\'s prior written consent.
Line 197: > \(c\) **New Environmental Remediation Contracts.** Do not enter into any new environmental remediation or response contract or agreement with a contract value exceeding \$500,000 (or such other threshold as may be agreed) without the buyer\'s prior written consent.
Line 199: > \(d\) **Environmental Insurance.** Maintain all environmental impairment liability insurance policies, pollution legal liability insurance policies, and contractor\'s pollution liability insurance policies in full force and effect, with coverage levels no less than those in effect as of the date of the agreement.
Line 201: > \(e\) **Notice of Environmental Claims.** Provide prompt written notice to the buyer (and in no event later than five (5) business days after the Company\'s receipt thereof) of any new environmental claim, notice of violation, information request under CERCLA Section 104(e), RCRA Section 3007, or any analogous state law provision, consent order, administrative complaint, or other regulatory action received by the Company during the Interim Period.
Line 203: > \(f\) **Settlement of Environmental Claims.** Do not settle, compler\'s draft SPA makes no reference to R&W Insurance or to the waiver of insurer subrogation rights, the associate must add an R&W Insurance subrogation waiver provision. In many transactions, the availability and structure of R&W Insurance is negotiated at the term-sheet level, and the subrogation waiver is a term-sheet-level commitment. Its omission from the SPA must be corrected. **Priority: HIGH.**
Line 431: **Sample Subrogation Waiver Language:**
Line 433: > *\"Buyer shall obtain and maintain a representations and warranties insurance policy (the \'R&W Insurance Policy\') and shall cause such R&W Insurance Policy to provide that the insurer thereunder shall waive, and shall not exercise or pursue, any right of subrogation or any other right of recovery against Seller or any of its Affiliates, directors, officers, employees, agents, or representatives with respect to any claim made by Buyer under such R&W Insurance Policy, except to the extent such claim arises from or relates to Fraud by Seller. Buyer shall not amend, modify, or waive any provision of the R&W Insurance Policy in a manner that would adversely affect Seller\'s rights under this Section \[\_\_\] without Seller\'s prior written consent.\"*
Line 435: **Coordination with Other Provisions.** The availability of R&W Insurance does not change the SPA\'s indemnification cap, escrow requirements, or other indemnification terms. The R&W Insurance policy is a supplement to the seller\'s direct indemnification obligations, not a substitute for them. Associates should resist any seller argument that the availability of R&W Insurance justifies a lower SPA indemnification cap or a smaller escrow.
Line 437: **[Section 9: Purchase Price Mechanics and Debt Payoff]{.underline}**
Line 451: **[9.2 Closing Indebtedness and Payoff Letters]{.underline}**
Line 455: The SPA must require the seller to deliver payoff letters from each holder of target indebtedness no later than three (3) business days prior to the scheduled closing date. Each payoff letter must include: (a) the total outstanding balance as of the anticipated closing date (including accrued and unpaid interest, prepayment premiums, breakage costs, and all other amounts necessary to fully satisfy the obligation); (b) wiring instructions for the payoff amount; and (c) an agreement by the lender to deliver lien release documentation (including UCC-3 termination statements, mortgage releases, and intellectual property lien releases, as applicable) promptly upon receipt of the payoff amount.
Line 457: Delivery of payoff letters meeting these requirements should be a condition to the buyer\'s obligation to close. If payoff letters are not delivered timely, the buyer should have the right to delay closing until they are delivered or, if the delay exceeds a specified number of business days, to terminate the agreement.
Line 479: **Lender Coordination.** The buyer\'s acquisition lender (e.g., Clearwater Environmental Lending Corp. or a similar specialty lender) will typically require payoff letters as a condition to funding the acquisition facility. The SPA\'s closing mechanics must align with the lender\'s requirements regarding the timing and content of payoff letters. Associates should obtain and review the buyer\'s lender\'s commitment letter to identify any specific payoff letter requirements and ensure that the SPA\'s closing conditions are consistent.
Line 481: **[Section 10: Non-Competition and Non-Solicitation Covenants]{.underline}**
Line 485: Non-competition and non-solicitation covenants are standard in PE acquisitions and are critical to protecting the buyer\'s investment in the acquired business. A well-drafted non-compete prevents the seller (and its principals) from establishing or participating in a competing business that could divert customers, employees, or business opportunities from the acquired company during the critical post-acquisition integration period.
Line 487: Associates should always cross-reference the executed term sheet for the agreed-upon non-compete parameters (duration, geographic scope, and business scope). The SPA\'s non-compete provisions must conform to the term sheet.
Line 489: **Firm Standard for Environmental Services Sector:**
Line 491: **Duration.** Two (2) to four (4) years post-closing. Three (3) years is the most common duration in recent environmental services transactions handled by the firm and is the firm\'s standard recommendation. Durations shorter than two years provide inadequate protection for the buyer\'s investment; durations longer than four years may raise enforceability concerns in certain jurisdictions.
Line 493: **Geographic Scope.** The non-compete should be limited to the states and jurisdictions in which the target conducts business as of the closing date, plus any states or jurisdictions in which the target has active proposals or bids pending as of the closing date. A nationwide non-compete is generally not advisable unless the target operates in a majority of states. An overbroad geographic restriction risks unenforceability --- courts in many jurisdictions will decline to enforce a non-compete with a geographic scope that is not reasonably tailored to the legitimate business interest being protected.
Line 495: **Business Scope.** The non-compete should be limited to the specific business lines of the target --- for example, \"environmental remediation services, hazardous waste management and transportation services, and environmental consulting and engineering services.\" The non-compete should not extend to \"any business\" or to business lines unrelated to the target\'s operations. Where the seller is a diversified holding company with business lines unrelated to the target (e.g., construction, timber management, real estate development), an overbroad non-compete could restrict legitimate seller activities and may be struck down by a court as unreasonable in its scope.
Line 497: **Enforceability Considerations.** Enforceability of non-compete covenants varies significantly by jurisdiction. Delaware courts generally enforce reasonable non-competition covenants entered into in connection with the sale of a business, applying a reasonableness standard that considers the duration, geographic scope, and business scope of the restriction in light of the legitimate interests being protected. Oregon courts similarly apply a reasonableness test but impose specific statutory requirements for non-compete agreements. Some jurisdictions (most notably California) are hostile to non-compete covenants generally, although the sale-of-business exception may apply. Associates should identify the governing law of the non-compete provision and confirm that the covenant\'s terms are consistent with the requirements of that jurisdiction. Overbroad covenants risk being voided entirely rather than judicially reformed, depending on the jurisdiction\'s approach to reformation (sometimes called \"blue penciling\").
Line 499: **Non-Solicitation.** In addition to the non-compete, the SPA should include non-solicitation covenants prohibiting the seller and its principals from (a) soliciting or hiring employees of the target and (b) soliciting or diverting customers or suppliers of the target. The non-solicitation period should match the non-compete period.
Line 501: **[Section 11: Knowledge Qualifiers and Other Definitional Issues]{.underline}**
Line 503: **[11.1 Knowledge Definition]{.underline}**
Line 505: The definition of \"Knowledge\" (or \"to the knowledge of the Seller/Company\") is used throughout the SPA to qualify certain representations and warranties. matches.line: **[M&A PLAYBOOK --- ENVIRONMENTAL SERVICES SECTOR ACQUISITIONS]{.underline}**
With contributions from the Environmental Regulatory Practice Group and the Government Contracts Practice Group

**NOTE:** This playbook supplements the Firm\'s General M&A Playbook (v.7.1) and should be read in conjunction with it. Where this sector-specific playbook addresses a topic also covered in the General Playbook, this playbook governs for environmental services transactions. In the event of any inconsistency between this playbook and the General M&A Playbook with respect to an environmental services acquisition, the guidance set forth in this playbook controls. Associates should maintain copies of both playbooks and consult both when reviewing or drafting transaction documents for environmental services targets.

This playbook provides comprehensive guidance to associates at Ashford, Pennington & Yates LLP who are reviewing, drafting, or marking up stock purchase agreements (\"SPAs\") and asset purchase agreements (\"APAs\") on behalf of private equity (\"PE\") buyer clients acquiring companies in the environmental services sector. For purposes of this playbook, \"environmental services\" encompasses a broad range of businesses, including environmental remediation, hazardous waste management, hazardous waste transportation, environmental consulting, environmental engineering, environmental testing and laboratory services, and related businesses.

Environmental services targets present unique and significant risks not commonly found in general middle-market transactions. Associates must be attentive to the following sector-specific risk categories, each of which is addressed in detail in subsequent sections of this playbook:

> \(i\) **Significant potential environmental liabilities** under the Comprehensive Environmental Response, Compensation, and Liability Act (\"CERCLA\"), the Resource Conservation and Recovery Act (\"RCRA\"), and state equivalents, which can result in strict, joint and several liability for contamination at sites where the target has operated, disposed of waste, or arranged for disposal;

> \(ii\) **Heavy regulatory permitting requirements**, including permits under RCRA, the Clean Air Act, the Clean Water Act, and various state environmental regulatory programs, many of which are subject to transfer or notification requirements upon a change of control;

> \(iii\) **Government contract exposure and anti-assignment rules**, as many environmental services companies derive significant revenue from federal, state, and local government contracts that are subject to the Anti-Assignment Act, Federal Acquisition Regulation (\"FAR\") novation requirements, and similar restrictions;

> \(iv\) **Key-person dependencies for professional licenses**, as environmental consulting and engineering businesses often depend on individuals holding professional engineer (\"PE\") licenses, professional geologist licenses, or other professional certifications that are personal to the individual and cannot be transferred; and

> \(v\) **Above-market affiliate transactions**, which are common in family-owned or closely held targets and which can distort EBITDA calculations and create ongoing post-closing value leakage if not properly addressed in the acquisition documentation.
This playbook is designed for the deal profile most commonly encountered by the firm\'s PE buyer clients in the environmental services sector. The typical transaction parameters are as follows:

**Enterprise Value Range.** Middle-market environmental services acquisitions with enterprise values typically ranging from \$75 million to \$500 million. The majority of transactions handled by the firm in this sector fall within the \$100 million to \$350 million range.

**Transaction Structure.** 100% stock purchase or asset purchase. Stock purchases are strongly preferred by PE buyers in this sector because a stock acquisition preserves the target entity\'s environmental permits, government contracts, and professional registrations without the need for transfer, novation, or re-issuance. Asset purchases may be required in certain circumstances, such as corporate divestitures where the target business is a division rather than a separate legal entity, or where the buyer wishes to avoid assuming certain liabilities. When an asset purchase structure is used, associates must pay particular attention to environmental permit transfer requirements and government contract assignment restrictions, both of which are more complex in asset deals.

**Seller Profile.** The seller is typically a founder-owned or family-owned holding company, a closely held group of shareholders, or a corporate parent divesting a non-core business line. Family-owned sellers are particularly common in the environmental services sector, as many environmental remediation and waste management companies were founded in the 1980s and 1990s during the initial wave of CERCLA enforcement and are now being sold by retiring founders. Associates should be alert to the dynamics of negotiating with founder-sellers, who may have strong emotional attachments to the business and who may insist on provisions that are not market-standard.

**Valuation.** Typical EBITDA multiples in the environmental services sector range from 5.5x to 7.5x Adjusted EBITDA, with the precise multiple depending on factors including geographic footprint, customer concentration, regulatory compliance history, government contract backlog, and growth trajectory. Premium multiples (above 7.0x) are typically reserved for targets with significant recurring revenue, diversified customer bases, and strong regulatory track records.

**Common EBITDA Adjustments.** The Adjusted EBITDA calculation in environmental services transactions commonly includes adjustments for: (a) above-market rent payments to seller-affiliated entities (which is one of the most significant adjustments in family-owned targets); (b) one-time litigation costs, including environmental litigation defense costs; (c) excess owner compensation (where the founder-owner draws a salary significantly above market for a comparable executive); (d) one-time transaction expenses; and (e) non-recurring regulatory compliance costs. Associates should review the quality of earnings report prepared by the buyer\'s financial advisor and ensure that the EBITDA adjustments reflected in the purchase price are properly addressed in the SPA\'s working capital methodology and affiliate transaction provisions.

**Buyer\'s Lender.** In many recent transactions, the buyer\'s acquisition financing has been provided by specialty lenders such as Clearwater Environmental Lending Corp. and similar institutions with sector expertise. These lenders impose additional requirements on deal documentation, including specific insurance requirements, environmental compliance covenants, and reporting obligations. Associates should obtain and review the lender\'s term sheet and commitment letter early in the drafting process and ensure that the SPA\'s closing mechanics, representations, and covenants are consistent with the lender\'s requirements.

> \(a\) **The executed term sheet** (or letter of intent), which is always the primary benchmark for the commercial terms of the transaction. Where the term sheet specifies a particular deal term (such as the indemnification cap or non-compete duration), the SPA must conform to the term sheet unless the responsible partner has authorized a deviation.

> \(b\) **The due diligence reports**, particularly the environmental due diligence memo, the regulatory compliance memo, and the government contracts memo. These reports identify specific risks that must be addressed in the SPA.
**[Section 2: Material Adverse Effect Definition]{.underline}**
**[2.1 Firm Standard on MAE Definitions]{.underline}**

The Material Adverse Effect (\"MAE\") definition is one of the most heavily negotiated provisions in any acquisition agreement and is critical to the buyer\'s closing conditions and representation structure. The MAE definition determines whether an adverse development at the target between signing and closing constitutes a material adverse change that would permit the buyer to decline to close, and it also qualifies many of the seller\'s representations and warranties (e.g., \"no events have occurred that have had or would reasonably be expected to have a Material Adverse Effect\"). Because of the MAE definition\'s outsized impact on the buyer\'s rights, associates must review it with extreme care.

The MAE definition should be narrowly tailored to capture genuine, target-specific material adverse changes in the business, operations, financial condition, assets, liabilities, or results of operations of the target company. The definition should be broad enough to encompass any type of material adverse development, without limiting the concept to a particular category of harm.

**Standard Carve-outs.** It is market practice for the MAE definition to include carve-outs (exclusions) for certain categories of changes or events that are beyond the target\'s control and that affect the broader economy or markets rather than the target specifically. The following carve-outs are generally acceptable:
> \(d\) Epidemics, pandemics, or other public health emergencies (including government responses thereto);

**THIS IS A CRITICAL REQUIREMENT.** All industry-specific carve-outs and regulatory carve-outs in the MAE definition MUST include a \"disproportionate impact\" exception. This is a firm-wide requirement and is non-negotiable for environmental services transactions. The standard formulation the firm requires is:

> *\"\...provided, however, that any change, effect, event, or development referred to in clauses (a) through (f) above shall be taken into account in determining whether a Material Adverse Effect has occurred or would reasonably be expected to occur to the extent such change, effect, event, or development disproportionately affects the Company and its Subsidiaries, taken as a whole, relative to other participants in the industries in which the Company and its Subsidiaries operate.\"*

**Rationale.** Without the disproportionate impact qualifier, industry-specific and regulatory carve-outs can effectively hollow out the MAE definition, rendering it meaningless. This risk is especially acute for environmental services companies. Consider the following scenario: if the MAE definition carves out \"changes in environmental laws or regulations\" or \"changes affecting the environmental services industry generally\" without a disproportionate impact qualifier, the seller could argue that virtually any adverse regulatory development --- including a new CERCLA regulation that specifically targets the target\'s disposal practices, a state-level ban on a waste treatment methodology that constitutes 40% of the target\'s revenue, or an EPA enforcement initiative directed at the specific category of environmental services the target provides --- is excluded from the MAE definition because it \"affects the environmental services industry generally\" or constitutes a \"change in environmental law.\" This interpretation would render the buyer\'s closing condition (no MAE since signing) essentially unenforceable, because the most likely sources of material adverse change for an environmental services company are precisely the regulatory and industry changes that the carve-out would exclude.

The disproportionate impact qualifier resolves this problem by providing that even if a change is of the type described in the carve-out (e.g., a general change in environmental law), it still counts toward the MAE analysis to the extent it disproportionately affects the target compared to other industry participants. This preserves the buyer\'s protection against target-specific harm while still excluding truly general, industry-wide developments that affect all participants equally.

**Specific Instruction.** If the seller\'s draft excludes \"changes in the environmental services industry generally\" or \"changes in environmental laws or regulations\" from the MAE definition without a disproportionate impact qualifier, this MUST be flagged and corrected. The associate should add the disproportionate impact qualifier language set forth above. **Priority: CRITICAL.**
**Example of Acceptable MAE Carve-out Language:**

> *\"\...provided, however, that none of the following shall be deemed to constitute, and none of the following shall be taken into account in determining whether there has been, a Material Adverse Effect: (a) changes in general economic conditions or conditions in the financial markets generally; (b) changes affecting the industries in which the Company operates generally; (c) changes in applicable Law (including Environmental Laws) or GAAP; (d) acts of war, armed hostilities, terrorism, or natural disasters; (e) epidemics, pandemics, or other public health emergencies; or (f) changes resulting from the announcement or pendency of the transactions contemplated hereby; provided, further, that, with respect to clauses (a) through (e), such changes, effects, events, or developments may be taken into account in determining whether a Material Adverse Effect has occurred or would reasonably be expected to occur to the extent that such changes, effects, events, or developments have a disproportionate effect on the Company and its Subsidiaries, taken as a whole, relative to other participants in the industries in which the Company and its Subsidiaries operate.\"*
**[2.2 Environmental-Sector-Specific MAE Considerations]{.underline}**

Beyond the general requirement for the disproportionate impact qualifier addressed in Section 2.1, associates must be attentive to several additional MAE issues that are unique to environmental services acquisitions.

**Regulatory Exposure.** Environmental services companies are uniquely exposed to regulatory changes that could devastate the target\'s value. Changes in CERCLA regulations, modifications to RCRA permitting requirements, new EPA enforcement policies, state-level environmental law changes, and shifts in regulatory interpretation can fundamentally alter the target\'s business model, cost structure, and liability exposure. A broadly worded regulatory carve-out without a disproportionate impact qualifier would allow the seller to argue that sweeping regulatory changes affecting the target --- even those directed specifically at the target\'s business practices --- are excluded from the MAE definition. This is precisely the scenario the disproportionate impact qualifier is designed to address, and its importance in the environmental services context cannot be overstated.

**Pending or Threatened Litigation.** Associates should carefully review whether the MAE definition carves out \"changes resulting from pending or threatened litigation.\" In many general middle-market transactions, this carve-out is unremarkable. However, for environmental services targets with known environmental exposure --- including targets that are potentially responsible parties (\"PRPs\") at CERCLA Superfund sites, targets with ongoing state environmental enforcement actions, or targets facing private contribution or cost-recovery claims --- a litigation carve-out could exclude from the MAE definition precisely the type of adverse development most likely to occur. If the target has known environmental litigation exposure, the associate should either (a) remove the litigation carve-out entirely, or (b) add an express exclusion to the litigation carve-out providing that it does not apply to environmental litigation or claims arising under CERCLA, RCRA, or state environmental law equivalents.

**CERCLA Exposure.** Specifically, exposures of the type associated with CERCLA response cost liability --- such as EPA information requests under CERCLA Section 104(e), PRP notification letters, unilateral administrative orders, and contributions to Superfund remediation costs --- should not be carved out of the MAE definition. These \"Dalton Creek-type\" CERCLA exposures (referring to the category of historical disposal site liabilities frequently encountered in environmental services due diligence) represent some of the most significant and unpredictable risks to environmental services companies, and the buyer must retain the ability to invoke the MAE closing condition if such liabilities materialize or escalate between signing and closing.

**Associates should confirm** that the MAE definition, read as a whole, does not inadvertently exclude from the MAE analysis the categories of adverse developments most relevant to the environmental services target being acquired. If in doubt, escalate to the responsible partner.

> \(b\) Use commercially reasonable efforts to maintain and preserve intact the business, operations, and relationships of the Company, including relationships with customers, suppliers, employees, and governmental authorities;
> \(c\) Maintain all insurance policies (including environmental impairment liability insurance) in full force and effect;
> \(e\) Comply in all material respects with all applicable laws, permits, and governmental orders;
> \(l\) Not create, incur, or permit any liens on the Company\'s assets (other than permitted liens); and

For environmental services targets, additional sector-specific covenants are required, as set forth in Section 3.3 below. Additionally, affiliate transaction restrictions --- which are critically important in this sector --- are addressed separately in Section 3.2 below.
**[3.2 Affiliate Transaction Restrictions]{.underline}**

**THIS IS A HIGH-PRIORITY REQUIREMENT.** The interim operating covenants MUST include a specific, express restriction prohibiting the target from entering into, amending, modifying, extending, renewing, or terminating any contract, transaction, or arrangement with the seller, any affiliate of the seller, or any officer, director, manager, member, shareholder, or family member of the seller or any seller affiliate, without the buyer\'s prior written consent (not to be unreasonably withheld, conditioned, or delayed).

**Rationale.** In acquisitions of family-owned or closely held environmental services targets, affiliate transactions represent a persistent and significant risk during the Interim Period. The selling shareholders and their affiliated entities frequently engage in transactions with the target that may not be at arm\'s length, and the risk of value extraction through affiliate transactions is heightened during the period between signing and closing, when the seller knows that it will shortly be relinquishing control of the business. Common abuses observed in environmental services transactions handled by the firm include:

> \(a\) **Increasing rent payments under affiliate leases.** Environmental services companies frequently lease office space, equipment yards, vehicle storage facilities, or waste disposal facilities from entities controlled by the selling shareholders. The seller may attempt to increase the rent under these leases during the Interim Period, extracting value from the target before the buyer takes control.

> \(b\) **Entering into new management or consulting agreements with seller-affiliated entities.** Sellers may attempt to create new contractual payment obligations running from the target to seller affiliates during the Interim Period, often styled as \"management fees,\" \"consulting arrangements,\" or \"transition services.\"
> \(c\) **Prepaying obligations to affiliates.** The target may accelerate payment of amounts owed to seller affiliates, depleting the target\'s cash and reducing net working capital.

> \(d\) **Extending the term of above-market affiliate contracts.** The seller may attempt to lock in above-market affiliate arrangements for extended periods, making them more difficult or expensive for the buyer to unwind post-closing.

**Specific Context for Environmental Services Deals.** In environmental services transactions, it is extremely common for the target to lease critical operational facilities --- including equipment yards, staging areas, waste storage facilities, and disposal sites --- from entities controlled by the selling shareholders. EBITDA adjustments for above-market affiliate rent are among the most common adjustments in this sector, with recent transactions handled by the firm reflecting above-market rent adjustments of \$1,600,000 or more. However, these EBITDA adjustments only protect the buyer on the purchase price (valuation) side --- they do not prevent the seller from increasing or adding affiliate payments during the Interim Period, which would reduce the target\'s cash flow and working capital independent of the valuation adjustment.
The affiliate transaction restriction covenant is the primary contractual mechanism to prevent this form of value leakage. Its inclusion in the SPA is mandatory. **Priority: HIGH.**
**Sample Affiliate Transaction Restriction Covenant:**

> *\"During the period from the date of this Agreement until the earlier of the Closing Date and the termination of this Agreement in accordance with its terms, the Company shall not, and Seller shall cause the Company not to, directly or indirectly, (a) enter into any Contract, transaction, or arrangement with, (b) amend, modify, extend, renew, or supplement any existing Contract, transaction, or arrangement with, (c) make any payment or transfer any asset to (other than compensation payments to employees in the ordinary course of business consistent with past practice), or (d) terminate any existing Contract with, in each case, Seller, any Affiliate of Seller, or any officer, director, manager, shareholder, member, partner, or family member (within the meaning of Section 267(c)(4) of the Code) of Seller or any Affiliate of Seller, in each case without the prior written consent of Buyer (which consent shall not be unreasonably withheld, conditioned, or delayed).\"*
**[3.3 Environmental-Sector-Specific Covenants]{.underline}**

In addition to the general interim operating covenants set forth in Section 3.1 and the affiliate transaction restrictions set forth in Section 3.2, the SPA for an environmental services acquisition must include the following sector-specific interim covenants:

> \(a\) **Environmental Permits.** Maintain all Environmental Permits in full force and effect; do not take any action, or fail to take any action, that could reasonably be expected to result in the revocation, suspension, modification, non-renewal, or material limitation of any Environmental Permit held by the Company.

> \(b\) **Active Remediation Projects.** Continue all active remediation and environmental response projects in the ordinary course of business and in compliance with all applicable orders, consent decrees, administrative agreements, remediation action plans, and other governmental requirements. Do not voluntarily suspend, terminate, or materially alter the scope of any active remediation project without the buyer\'s prior written consent.

> \(c\) **New Environmental Remediation Contracts.** Do not enter into any new environmental remediation or response contract or agreement with a contract value exceeding \$500,000 (or such other threshold as may be agreed) without the buyer\'s prior written consent.

> \(d\) **Environmental Insurance.** Maintain all environmental impairment liability insurance policies, pollution legal liability insurance policies, and contractor\'s pollution liability insurance policies in full force and effect, with coverage levels no less than those in effect as of the date of the agreement.

> \(e\) **Notice of Environmental Claims.** Provide prompt written notice to the buyer (and in no event later than five (5) business days after the Company\'s receipt thereof) of any new environmental claim, notice of violation, information request under CERCLA Section 104(e), RCRA Section 3007, or any analogous state law provision, consent order, administrative complaint, or other regulatory action received by the Company during the Interim Period.

> \(f\) **Settlement of Environmental Claims.** Do not settle, compromise, or consent to the entry of any judgment with respect to any environmental claim, proceeding, or regulatory action involving potential liability in excess of \$250,000 (or such other threshold as may be agreed) without the buyer\'s prior written consent.

Associates should review the environmental due diligence memo for a list of all active remediation projects, environmental permits, and pending environmental claims, and confirm that the interim covenants adequately cover each identified item.

The survival period for representations and warranties determines the window during which the buyer may assert indemnification claims for breaches of those representations. The survival framework is one of the most commercially significant elements of the indemnification structure and must be carefully reviewed in every transaction.
The firm\'s standard survival framework for PE acquisitions in the environmental services sector is as follows:

**General Representations.** All other representations and warranties (other than Fundamental Representations, Tax Representations, and Environmental Representations, which are addressed in Section 4.2 below) should survive for a period of eighteen (18) to twenty-four (24) months post-closing. The market range for general representation survival in middle-market PE transactions is fifteen (15) to twenty-four (24) months. A survival period within this range is acceptable. A survival period below fifteen (15) months should be pushed back, as it provides the buyer with insufficient time to discover breaches, particularly breaches that may not become apparent until the buyer has operated the business through a full annual cycle. The firm\'s preferred position is twenty-four (24) months.

**Independence of Basket and Survival.** Associates should note that the basket (deductible) structure is independent of the survival period. Claims must be asserted during the applicable survival period (i.e., the buyer must provide written notice of a claim before the survival period expires), but the basket is a separate limitation on recovery that operates independently. A claim timely asserted during the survival period is not extinguished merely because the aggregate basket threshold has not yet been met; rather, timely-asserted claims accumulate and become recoverable once the basket threshold is satisfied.

**Basket Standard.** For reference (this topic is addressed in detail in Section 5.2), a true deductible of 0.75% to 1.0% of enterprise value is market-standard for middle-market transactions in the environmental services sector. A basket within this range should generally be accepted without markup, as discussed further in Section 11.2.
**[4.2 Environmental Representations --- Extended Survival]{.underline}**

**THIS IS A CRITICAL REQUIREMENT.** For targets in the environmental services sector, environmental representations --- including but not limited to representations regarding environmental compliance, Environmental Permits, hazardous materials and hazardous waste management, CERCLA and Superfund matters, environmental remediation obligations, environmental insurance, and environmental litigation --- MUST survive for a minimum of thirty-six (36) months post-closing. The firm\'s preferred position is survival for the full applicable statute of limitations (which, for CERCLA claims, is effectively indefinite, as CERCLA imposes strict, joint and several liability with no statute of repose in many circumstances).

**Rationale.** Environmental liabilities under CERCLA, RCRA, and state environmental law equivalents frequently take years --- and in some cases, decades --- to manifest fully. The lifecycle of a typical CERCLA enforcement action illustrates this point:

Given this timeline, a twelve-month survival period for environmental representations in an environmental services acquisition is grossly inadequate and well below market expectations for this sector. A buyer who discovers a previously undisclosed CERCLA exposure fifteen months after closing --- a timeline that is entirely typical --- would have no indemnification recourse under a twelve-month survival provision. This outcome is unacceptable for PE buyer clients and does not reflect the risk profile of the sector.

**Specific Instruction.** If the seller\'s draft provides for a general twelve-month or shorter survival period that applies to environmental representations without differentiation, this MUST be flagged and corrected. At minimum, environmental representations should be carved out of the general representation survival period and given an independent survival period of thirty-six (36) months post-closing. Ideally, push for survival for the full applicable statute of limitations. If the seller resists the full statute of limitations, thirty-six months is the firm\'s minimum acceptable position. **Priority: CRITICAL.**

**Coordination with Escrow Release.** The environmental representation survival period must be coordinated with the escrow release schedule (see Section 5.4 below). Escrow funds designated for environmental representation claims should not be released before the expiration of the environmental representation survival period. If the general escrow is scheduled for release at eighteen (18) months post-closing but the environmental representation survival extends to thirty-six (36) months, the SPA must provide for a separate environmental escrow holdback that is maintained through the thirty-sixth month (less any amounts reserved for pending claims).

**Coordination with Special Indemnity.** The environmental representation survival period is separate from and in addition to the Special Indemnity for known environmental liabilities (see Section 6 below). The Special Indemnity addresses specifically identified environmental matters with a separate seventy-two (72) month survival period. The environmental representation survival period addresses breaches of the environmental representations generally --- i.e., undisclosed environmental liabilities and inaccuracies in the environmental representations that are not covered by the Special Indemnity.
**[Section 5: Indemnification Structure]{.underline}**
**[5.1 Indemnification Cap]{.underline}**
**THIS IS A CRITICAL REQUIREMENT.** The general indemnification cap is one of the most significant economic terms in the SPA and must conform precisely to the executed term sheet.

**Firm Standard.** For middle-market PE acquisitions in the \$100 million to \$500 million enterprise value range, the general indemnification cap should be set at 10% to 15% of the base enterprise value. The firm\'s target for PE buyer clients is 12.5% of enterprise value. This percentage represents the firm\'s standard recommendation based on extensive experience in environmental services transactions and is consistent with prevailing market data for the sector.

**Key Instruction.** Associates must always cross-reference the executed term sheet for the agreed-upon indemnification cap percentage. The term sheet is the governing benchmark for all commercial terms, and the indemnification cap is among the most carefully negotiated terms at the LOI stage. If the seller\'s draft SPA sets the general indemnification cap at a percentage different from what was agreed in the term sheet, this MUST be flagged immediately and corrected to match the term sheet. Do not accept any deviation from the term sheet cap without express written authorization from the responsible partner. This is a **Critical** priority item.

For example, if the term sheet specifies a general indemnification cap of 12.5% of enterprise value for a transaction with a \$200 million enterprise value, the SPA\'s general indemnification cap should be \$25,000,000. If the seller\'s draft sets the cap at \$20,000,000 (10% of enterprise value), the associate must flag this as a deviation from the term sheet and mark up the draft to reflect the agreed \$25,000,000 cap.

**R&W Insurance Considerations.** In transactions where the buyer is obtaining representations and warranties insurance (see Section 8), the indemnification cap may be subject to additional negotiation dynamics. The R&W insurer may require a certain retention level (the amount of loss the buyer must bear before the policy responds), which interacts with the SPA\'s basket/deductible and cap structure. However, the SPA cap itself must conform to the term sheet regardless of the R&W Insurance structure. The R&W Insurance policy supplements the seller\'s indemnification obligations --- it does not replace them, and the availability of insurance does not justify a reduction in the SPA cap below the term sheet level.

**Market Data.** In recent environmental services transactions handled by the firm, general indemnification caps have ranged from 10% to 15% of enterprise value. The 12.5% figure is squarely within the market range and represents the firm\'s standard recommendation for PE buyers in this sector. Caps below 10% of enterprise value are below market for environmental services acquisitions and should not be accepted without partner authorization. Caps at the higher end of the range (15%) may be appropriate for transactions with elevated environmental risk profiles.

**Escrow Mechanics.** The escrow amount (typically 7.5% of enterprise value --- see Section 5.4 for details) does NOT limit the buyer\'s right to recover under the indemnification provisions. For non-Fundamental Representation claims, the escrow is the first source of recovery, but the buyer\'s right to indemnification extends to the full amount of the general cap. Claims exceeding the escrow may be pursued directly against the seller (or, in the case of an equity rollover, may be offset against future payments) up to the general cap amount. The SPA must clearly and unambiguously state that the escrow does not constitute a limitation on the buyer\'s indemnification rights and that the buyer may pursue claims directly against the seller for amounts exceeding the escrow balance, up to the general indemnification cap. Any language in the seller\'s draft that could be interpreted as limiting the buyer\'s recovery to the escrow amount must be struck.
**[5.2 Basket / Deductible]{.underline}**

**Firm Standard.** A true deductible (not a tipping basket) of 0.75% to 1.0% of enterprise value is the market standard for middle-market transactions in the environmental services sector. Under a true deductible structure, the buyer bears the first dollar of indemnifiable losses up to the deductible amount; once the aggregate losses exceed the deductible, the buyer recovers only the excess over the deductible amount (not the full amount of losses from the first dollar). This is distinguished from a \"tipping basket\" (also called a \"threshold\" or \"first dollar\" basket), under which the basket functions as a threshold --- once aggregate losses exceed the basket amount, the buyer recovers the full amount of losses from the first dollar.
**Carve-outs from the Basket.** The following categories of claims must be carved out of (i.e., not subject to) the basket. This is non-negotiable:
> \(c\) Special Indemnities for known environmental liabilities (see Section 6); and
