Line 9: **FROM:** Environmental Practice Group, Ashford, Pennington & Yates LLP
Line 13: **RE:** Environmental Due Diligence Summary --- Acquisition of Cascadia Environmental Solutions, Inc. by Whitmore Capital Partners LLC
Line 17: This memorandum summarizes the findings and recommendations of the Environmental Practice Group arising from our environmental due diligence review of Cascadia Environmental Solutions, Inc. in connection with the proposed acquisition by Whitmore Capital Partners LLC. This memo is intended to inform the deal team\'s review of the Seller\'s Stock Purchase Agreement draft, which we understand will be circulated on or about October 22, 2025. All findings and recommendations set forth herein should be incorporated into the firm\'s SPA markup and negotiation strategy.
Line 21: Ashford, Pennington & Yates LLP\'s Environmental Practice Group has completed its environmental due diligence review of Cascadia Environmental Solutions, Inc. (\"Cascadia\" or the \"Company\"), an Oregon corporation headquartered at 8700 SW Tualatin-Sherwood Road, Suite 200, Tualatin, Oregon 97062. Cascadia provides environmental remediation, hazardous waste management, and environmental consulting services, operating through seven offices located in Oregon, Washington, California, and Nevada. The Company employs approximately 340 full-time employees across these operations.
Line 25: Our environmental due diligence review has identified four principal areas of environmental concern that the deal team must address in the Stock Purchase Agreement:
Line 27: 1\. **Dalton Creek CERCLA Exposure (HIGH RISK).** The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency has issued an information request under CERCLA § 104(e) to Cascadia regarding the Company\'s former operations at the Dalton Creek disposal facility. Although no formal enforcement action or PRP designation has been issued to date, the § 104(e) letter is a well-recognized precursor to potential enforcement activity. We estimate Cascadia\'s potential liability exposure in the range of \$1,500,000 to \$6,000,000, depending upon EPA\'s cost allocation approach and the solvency of other potentially responsible parties.
Line 29: 2\. **Hargrove Industrial Site Remediation (MODERATE RISK).** Cascadia is actively performing environmental remediation at the former Hargrove Industrial Site in Milwaukie, Oregon, under contract with the Oregon Department of Environmental Quality. Estimated remaining remediation costs total approximately \$4,200,000. This exposure is a contractual obligation and is covered by a site-specific environmental liability insurance policy with a \$10,000,000 policy limit, which appears adequate.
Line 31: 3\. **Environmental Permit Portfolio (MODERATE RISK).** Cascadia holds 23 active environmental permits across four states. Although the transaction is structured as a stock purchase, multiple state environmental regulatory programs require notification to or approval from the issuing agency upon a change in control of the permit holder. Failure to comply with these requirements could result in permit violations, enforcement actions, or permit revocation.
Line 33: 4\. **Government Contract Regulatory Compliance (HIGH RISK).** Cascadia is party to four active government contracts with the Oregon DEQ, Washington Department of Ecology, the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, and the Bureau of Land Management. The two federal contracts are subject to the Anti-Assignment Act and the Federal Acquisition Regulation\'s novation requirements under FAR Part 42, Subpart 42.12. Failure to obtain required novations could result in contract termination, eliminating a material revenue stream.
Line 35: This memorandum provides detailed findings for each of these areas and sets forth **specific recommendations for SPA provisions** that the deal team should incorporate into its markup of the Seller\'s draft agreement. These recommendations are informed by the executed term sheet dated September 10, 2025, applicable federal and state environmental law, and industry practice for acquisitions in the environmental services sector.
Line 39: Our environmental due diligence review was conducted between August 20, 2025 and October 15, 2025, following execution of the Letter of Intent between Whitmore Capital Partners LLC and Evergreen Holdings Group, Inc. on August 15, 2025. The following materials and information sources were reviewed in connection with this memorandum:
Line 41: > • **Environmental Site Assessments.** Phase I and Phase II environmental site assessments for all seven of the Company\'s office and operational locations in Oregon, Washington, California, and Nevada.
Line 43: > • **Environmental Permits.** Copies of all 23 active environmental remediation permits held by the Company across four states, including RCRA permits, NPDES permits, Clean Air Act emissions permits, state hazardous waste transporter permits, and state remediation contractor licenses.
Line 45: > • **Compliance Records.** Environmental compliance records, agency inspection reports, and notices of violation received by the Company for the preceding five-year period (2020--2025).
Line 47: > • **CERCLA Correspondence.** The EPA\'s CERCLA § 104(e) information request regarding the Dalton Creek disposal facility, dated February 12, 2025, together with the Company\'s written response thereto and all related internal correspondence and records.
Line 49: > • **Remediation Contracts.** All remediation contracts, statements of work, and work plans pertaining to the Hargrove Industrial Site remediation project, including the master contract with the Oregon Department of Environmental Quality and applicable task orders.
Line 51: > • **Insurance Policies.** Environmental impairment liability insurance policies issued by Northshore Specialty Insurance Co. to the Company, including the general environmental impairment liability policy (aggregate limit of \$15,000,000; per-occurrence limit of \$5,000,000) and the site-specific environmental liability insurance policy covering the Hargrove Industrial Site (policy limit of \$10,000,000).
Line 53: > • **Government Contracts.** Copies of all four active government contracts between the Company and the Oregon DEQ, Washington Department of Ecology, U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, and Bureau of Land Management, including all modifications, amendments, and task orders.
Line 57: > • **Professional Licenses.** Records pertaining to professional engineer (PE) licenses held by 12 employees identified as critical to maintaining permit compliance and performing permitted activities.
Line 59: > • **Financial Records.** Records obtained from Winslow & Tate CPA Group, the Company\'s independent auditor, relating to environmental liability accruals reflected in the Company\'s financial statements.
Line 63: **[III. Dalton Creek Disposal Facility --- CERCLA Exposure]{.underline}**
Line 67: Cascadia formerly operated at the Dalton Creek disposal facility, a former hazardous waste disposal site located in Clackamas County, Oregon. The Company\'s operations at Dalton Creek involved the handling, treatment, and disposal of hazardous wastes generated by third-party industrial customers. These operations significantly predate the current management team and were conducted during a period when the Company was under different operational leadership. According to records produced during due diligence and confirmed by management interviews, Cascadia ceased all operations at the Dalton Creek disposal facility in approximately 2015.
Line 69: In February 2025, the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, Region 10, issued an information request to Cascadia under Section 104(e) of the Comprehensive Environmental Response, Compensation, and Liability Act of 1980, as amended (\"CERCLA\"), 42 U.S.C. § 9604(e). The information request seeks comprehensive documentation of the Company\'s waste handling and disposal activities at the Dalton Creek facility, including waste manifests, disposal records, volume and characterization data, and operational history during the period of the Company\'s use of the site.
Line 71: As of the date of this memorandum, no formal enforcement action, notice of potential responsible party (\"PRP\") designation, unilateral administrative order, or lawsuit has been filed or issued by EPA or any other party against Cascadia in connection with the Dalton Creek facility. However, the issuance of a § 104(e) information request is widely recognized as a standard precursor to potential PRP designation and subsequent enforcement activity under CERCLA. The Company\'s management confirmed that it has retained outside environmental counsel to assist with the response to the information request and to monitor developments at the site.
Line 73: **[B. Estimated Liability Exposure]{.underline}**
Line 75: Based on our review of the Company\'s records, the EPA information request and the Company\'s response, publicly available site information, and consultation with environmental counsel experienced in CERCLA cost allocation proceedings, we estimate Cascadia\'s potential liability exposure in connection with the Dalton Creek disposal facility to be in the range of **\$1,500,000 to \$6,000,000**. The factors underlying this range are as follows:
Line 77: > • **Low End (\$1,500,000).** This estimate assumes that EPA pursues a multi-party cost allocation among all identified potentially responsible parties at the Dalton Creek site, that Cascadia\'s proportionate share of total cleanup costs is determined on the basis of the volume and toxicity of waste it disposed at the facility, and that other identified PRPs remain solvent and capable of bearing their respective shares. Under this scenario, Cascadia\'s share would represent a minority allocation consistent with its relative contribution to site contamination.
Line 79: > • **High End (\$6,000,000).** This estimate reflects the possibility that EPA may designate Cascadia as a major contributor to the contamination at the site, or that one or more other PRPs may prove financially unable to satisfy their allocated shares. Under CERCLA § 107, liability is joint and several, meaning that EPA may seek recovery of the full cost of remediation from any single PRP, regardless of that party\'s proportionate contribution. If other PRPs are insolvent or unidentifiable, Cascadia\'s exposure could increase significantly. The high-end estimate also accounts for the possibility that the overall scope and cost of site remediation may exceed current projections.
Line 81: It is important to note that CERCLA proceedings frequently extend over many years. Under CERCLA § 113(g)(2), the statute of limitations for a cost recovery action is six years from the date of completion of a remedial action at the site. Contribution claims under § 113(f) may extend further depending on the timing of settlement or judgment. Given that no formal remedial action has been initiated at the Dalton Creek site, it is possible that Cascadia\'s ultimate liability will not be determined for a period of years following the closing of the proposed transaction.
Line 83: The Company\'s environmental impairment liability insurance with Northshore Specialty Insurance Co. (aggregate limit \$15,000,000; per-occurrence limit \$5,000,000) may provide coverage for defense costs and some portion of the Company\'s ultimate liability in connection with the Dalton Creek matter. However, coverage for legacy disposal operations is commonly subject to policy exclusions, including prior-knowledge exclusions, pollution date restrictions, and exclusions for known or disclosed conditions. We recommend that insurance counsel conduct a detailed review of the applicable policy terms to determine the extent and reliability of available coverage.
Line 85: **[C. SPA Recommendations --- Dalton Creek]{.underline}**
Line 87: Based on the foregoing analysis, we make the following recommendations with respect to the treatment of the Dalton Creek CERCLA exposure in the Stock Purchase Agreement:
Line 89: **Recommendation 1 --- Special Indemnity.** Given the magnitude of the potential exposure (\$1,500,000 to \$6,000,000), the fact that this is a known and disclosed environmental liability arising from Seller\'s period of ownership, and the inherent uncertainty and protracted timeline of CERCLA proceedings, we **strongly recommend** that the SPA include a **Special Indemnity** obligating Seller to indemnify Buyer for all Losses arising from or related to the Dalton Creek disposal facility and the EPA\'s CERCLA § 104(e) information request, including without limitation all costs of investigation, remediation, defense, settlement, contribution, and related administrative proceedings. The Special Indemnity should be structured as follows:
Line 91: > \(a\) **Survival Period.** The Special Indemnity should survive for no less than **72 months** following the closing date, in order to account for the characteristically lengthy timeline of CERCLA proceedings and the six-year statute of limitations for CERCLA cost recovery actions under § 113(g)(2). A shorter survival period would create an unacceptable risk that Buyer\'s indemnification rights expire before a formal CERCLA claim crystallizes.
Line 93: > \(b\) **Exclusion from General Basket and Cap.** The Special Indemnity should **not** be subject to the general indemnification deductible basket or aggregate liability cap. The Dalton Creek matter is a known, quantifiable exposure that should be indemnified on a dollar-for-dollar basis from the first dollar of Loss. Subjecting this exposure to general basket and cap limitations would improperly shift a portion of the known risk to Buyer.
Line 95: > \(c\) **Escrow Holdback.** The Special Indemnity should be supported by a dedicated portion of the **escrow holdback** maintained with Pinnacle Trust Company for a minimum period of **36 months** following closing. The escrowed amount should be sufficient to cover at least the low end of the estimated liability range (\$1,500,000), with the full Special Indemnity obligation surviving for the 72-month period regardless of the release of escrowed funds.
Line 97: > \(d\) **Consistency with Term Sheet.** We note that the executed term sheet dated September 10, 2025, between Whitmore Capital Partners LLC and Evergreen Holdings Group, Inc., specifically provides for a \"Special Indemnity\" to address the Dalton Creek matter. The SPA must implement this agreed-upon commercial term. Omission of the Special Indemnity from the Seller\'s initial SPA draft would represent a departure from the agreed deal terms.
Line 99: **Recommendation 2 --- Extended Survival of Environmental Representations.** Independent of and in addition to the Dalton Creek Special Indemnity, the environmental representations and warranties in the SPA should survive for a minimum of **36 months** post-closing, and ideally for the **full applicable statute of limitations** for environmental claims. We understand that seller-favorable first drafts in the middle market typically propose a 12-month survival period for representations and warranties, including environmental representations. For a company whose core business is the provision of environmental remediation and hazardous waste management services, a 12-month survival period for environmental representations would be wholly inadequate for the following reasons:
Line 101: > \(a\) The Dalton Creek CERCLA exposure may not crystallize into a formal claim, enforcement action, or PRP designation for a period of years following closing, as discussed in Section III.B above.
Line 103: > \(b\) Cascadia\'s active remediation projects, including the Hargrove Industrial Site project, have multi-year performance timelines during which new environmental liabilities or breaches of environmental representations may emerge.
Line 105: > \(c\) Environmental liabilities in the remediation services sector routinely emerge well beyond a 12-month period due to the nature of contamination migration, delayed regulatory action, and evolving site characterization data.
Line 107: > \(d\) For a company whose entire value proposition is built upon environmental compliance and permitting, the environmental representations are among the most critical representations in the agreement and should be afforded extended protection commensurate with that importance.
Line 109: We recommend that the deal team take a firm position on extended survival of environmental representations during SPA negotiations.
Line 111: **[IV. Hargrove Industrial Site Remediation]{.underline}**
Line 115: Cascadia is currently performing active environmental remediation at the former Hargrove Industrial Site, located in Milwaukie, Oregon, under a remediation services contract with the Oregon Department of Environmental Quality (\"Oregon DEQ\"). The Hargrove project involves soil and groundwater remediation activities at the former industrial site, including excavation and off-site disposal of contaminated soil, installation and operation of a groundwater extraction and treatment system, and ongoing environmental monitoring. The Company estimates the total remaining cost to complete the remediation at approximately **\$4,200,000**, with the project expected to continue for approximately 18 to 24 months beyond the anticipated closing date. The Hargrove remediation contract is one of the Company\'s four active government contracts and represents a significant ongoing commitment of Company resources and personnel.
Line 119: Cascadia carries a site-specific environmental liability insurance policy issued by **Northshore Specialty Insurance Co.** with a **\$10,000,000 policy limit** specifically covering the Hargrove Industrial Site remediation project. This policy provides coverage for remediation costs, cost overruns, and third-party claims arising from the Company\'s remediation activities at the Hargrove site. Separately, the Company\'s broader environmental impairment liability insurance with Northshore Specialty Insurance Co. carries an aggregate limit of \$15,000,000 and a per-occurrence limit of \$5,000,000. The site-specific Hargrove policy appears adequate to cover the estimated remaining \$4,200,000 remediation cost plus potential cost overruns and third-party claims, assuming no policy exclusions or coverage defenses are applicable. We recommend that the SPA include a representation that all environmental insurance policies maintained by the Company are in full force and effect, that all premiums due have been paid, and that no notice of cancellation, non-renewal, or material modification has been received. The SPA should also include a pre-closing covenant requiring the Company to maintain all such policies through and following the closing date.
Line 123: We assess the Hargrove Industrial Site remediation project as a **moderate risk** item. The project is a standard remediation engagement being performed under a government contract with the Oregon DEQ. The principal risks are (i) cost overruns in excess of the current \$4,200,000 estimate, (ii) potential regulatory enforcement action if the Company fails to meet remediation milestones established in the work plan and consent order, and (iii) third-party claims arising from remediation activities. The available insurance coverage appears adequate to mitigate these risks. We note that the Oregon DEQ contract under which the Hargrove work is being performed is one of the four government contracts requiring novation or consent analysis, as discussed in Section VI below.
Line 125: **[V. Environmental Permit Portfolio]{.underline}**
Line 127: **[A. Overview of Permits]{.underline}**
Line 129: Cascadia holds **23 active environmental remediation permits** across four states: Oregon, Washington, California, and Nevada. The permit portfolio includes the following categories:
Line 131: > • **RCRA Permits.** Treatment, storage, and disposal (TSD) facility permits issued under the Resource Conservation and Recovery Act and corresponding state programs, authorizing the Company to handle, treat, store, and dispose of hazardous wastes at specified locations.
Line 133: > • **Clean Water Act Discharge Permits.** National Pollutant Discharge Elimination System (NPDES) permits authorizing the Company to discharge treated water and stormwater from remediation project sites in compliance with applicable effluent limitations.
Line 135: > • **Clean Air Act Emissions Permits.** Permits authorizing air emissions from remediation equipment, thermal treatment units, and related operations at Company facilities and project sites.
Line 137: > • **State Hazardous Waste Transporter Permits.** Permits issued by state environmental agencies authorizing the Company to transport hazardous waste within and between states.
Line 139: > • **State Remediation Contractor Licenses and Permits.** State-specific licenses and permits required to perform environmental remediation and hazardous waste management services as a licensed contractor.
Line 141: All 23 permits are held in the name of Cascadia Environmental Solutions, Inc. In addition, 12 of the Company\'s employees hold professional engineer (\"PE\") licenses that are critical to maintaining permit compliance and performing permitted activities. Several of the Company\'s permits are conditioned upon the availability of a PE-licensed professional to oversee permitted operations. Loss of these PE-licensed employees, whether through attrition, termination, or failure to transfer to the post-closing entity, could jeopardize the Company\'s standing under certain permits and impair its ability to perform permitted work.
Line 145: Although this transaction is structured as a **stock purchase** --- and therefore the legal entity holding the permits (Cascadia Environmental Solutions, Inc.) will not change --- many state environmental regulatory programs nonetheless require **notification to or approval from the issuing agency** upon a change in the ownership or control of the permit holder. This is a critical issue that must be addressed in the SPA. The applicable state-specific requirements include:
Line 147: > • **Oregon.** Oregon DEQ regulations require notification of a change of ownership or control of a permitted facility within 30 days of such change. Certain RCRA permits issued by Oregon DEQ may require formal transfer approval prior to the change taking effect. *See* OAR Chapter 340, Division 012 and applicable permit conditions.
Line 149: > • **Washington.** The Washington Department of Ecology requires prior written notification for changes in control of permitted entities. Certain permits include conditions that expressly require agency approval of ownership changes before the transfer is deemed valid. *See* WAC Chapter 173-303 and applicable permit conditions.
Line 151: > • **California.** The California Department of Toxic Substances Control (\"DTSC\") and regional water quality control boards often require notification and, in certain permit categories, prior approval for changes in control of entities holding hazardous waste facility permits and waste discharge requirements. The specific requirements vary by permit type and issuing authority.
Line 153: > • **Nevada.** The Nevada Division of Environmental Protection requires notification of ownership changes for certain categories of environmental permits, including hazardous waste management permits and water pollution control permits.
Line 155: Even in a stock acquisition, these agencies may treat a change of the ultimate parent company --- here, the acquisition of Cascadia\'s shares by Whitmore Capital Partners LLC from Evergreen Holdings Group, Inc. --- as a \"change of ownership or control\" that triggers notification or approval requirements under the applicable permit or regulation. Failure to comply with these requirements could result in permit violations, enforcement actions, fines, or in extreme cases, permit revocation or suspension. Given that Cascadia\'s business is entirely dependent upon its ability to perform work under these permits, any disruption to the permit portfolio would be material.
Line 157: We anticipate that the Seller\'s SPA draft, once circulated, will include representations that all necessary environmental permits are held by the Company and are in good standing. However, a mere representation regarding the current status of permits is insufficient to protect Buyer from the risks associated with the change-of-control process. We **strongly recommend** that the SPA include the following provisions:
Line 159: > \(a\) **Pre-Closing Covenant.** A covenant requiring Seller and the Company, prior to closing, to (i) identify all environmental permits that require change-of-control notification to or approval from the issuing agency, (ii) prepare and submit all required notifications and applications for approval to the appropriate state environmental agencies, and (iii) cooperate with Buyer in providing all information reasonably requested by any such agency in connection with the change-of-control process.
Line 161: > \(b\) **Post-Closing Cooperation Covenant.** A covenant obligating Seller to cooperate with Buyer following closing in completing any permit transfer, re-issuance, amendment, or notification process required by any governmental authority as a result of the change of control, including executing documents, providing historical information, and participating in agency proceedings as reasonably requested by Buyer.
Line 163: > \(c\) **Survival.** These covenants should survive closing for at least **12 months**, or such longer period as may be necessary to complete all pending permit transfers and notifications, including any pending agency review or approval processes.
Line 165: Affirmative covenants addressing the permit transfer and notification process are essential to protect Buyer\'s investment in a business whose value depends on the continuity of its environmental permits.
Line 167: **[VI. Government Contract Regulatory Requirements]{.underline}**
Line 169: **[A. Overview of Government Contracts]{.underline}**
Line 171: Cascadia is party to **four active government contracts**, each of which is material to the Company\'s operations and revenue:
Line 173: > 1\. **Oregon Department of Environmental Quality** --- Environmental remediation services, including the Hargrove Industrial Site remediation project discussed in Section IV above.
Line 175: > 2\. **Washington Department of Ecology** --- Environmental consulting and remediation services at multiple sites within the State of Washington.
Line 177: > 3\. **U.S. Army Corps of Engineers** --- Environmental assessment and remediation services at federally owned or managed properties.
Line 179: > 4\. **Bureau of Land Management** --- Environmental site characterization and remediation services on federal lands managed by BLM.
Line 181: These four government contracts collectively represent a material portion of Cascadia\'s annual revenue and serve as a foundation for the Company\'s ongoing business operations. Loss of any one or more of these contracts would have a material adverse effect on the Company\'s financial condition and business prospects.
Line 183: **[B. Anti-Assignment Act and FAR Novation Requirements]{.underline}**
Line 185: Federal government contracts are subject to the **Anti-Assignment Act, 41 U.S.C. § 6305**, which generally prohibits the transfer or assignment of government contracts without the consent of the contracting officer. While the Anti-Assignment Act has historically been interpreted to apply primarily to assignments of the contract itself (as opposed to changes in corporate ownership), the **Federal Acquisition Regulation (\"FAR\"), Part 42, Subpart 42.12**, specifically addresses changes in the contractor\'s organizational structure, including changes in ownership.
Line 187: Under **FAR 42.1204**, when a contractor undergoes a change in ownership --- including when a third party acquires the stock of the contractor --- the contractor is required to submit a request for a **novation agreement** (or, in some cases, a **change-of-name agreement**) to the responsible contracting officer. A novation agreement formally recognizes the successor entity and transfers the government\'s contractual rights and obligations to the recognized successor. The key requirements under FAR 42.12 include:
Line 189: > • **FAR 42.1204(a).** The contractor must submit a written request for novation to the responsible contracting officer, accompanied by supporting documentation including the acquisition agreement (or relevant portions thereof), a list of all affected contracts, and evidence of the transferee\'s technical and financial capability to perform.
Line 191: > • **FAR 42.1204(e).** The contracting officer must make an affirmative determination that recognizing the successor is in the government\'s interest before executing the novation agreement.

matches.line: **FROM:** Environmental Practice Group, Ashford, Pennington & Yates LLP
**RE:** Environmental Due Diligence Summary --- Acquisition of Cascadia Environmental Solutions, Inc. by Whitmore Capital Partners LLC

This memorandum summarizes the findings and recommendations of the Environmental Practice Group arising from our environmental due diligence review of Cascadia Environmental Solutions, Inc. in connection with the proposed acquisition by Whitmore Capital Partners LLC. This memo is intended to inform the deal team\'s review of the Seller\'s Stock Purchase Agreement draft, which we understand will be circulated on or about October 22, 2025. All findings and recommendations set forth herein should be incorporated into the firm\'s SPA markup and negotiation strategy.

Ashford, Pennington & Yates LLP\'s Environmental Practice Group has completed its environmental due diligence review of Cascadia Environmental Solutions, Inc. (\"Cascadia\" or the \"Company\"), an Oregon corporation headquartered at 8700 SW Tualatin-Sherwood Road, Suite 200, Tualatin, Oregon 97062. Cascadia provides environmental remediation, hazardous waste management, and environmental consulting services, operating through seven offices located in Oregon, Washington, California, and Nevada. The Company employs approximately 340 full-time employees across these operations.
Our environmental due diligence review has identified four principal areas of environmental concern that the deal team must address in the Stock Purchase Agreement:

1\. **Dalton Creek CERCLA Exposure (HIGH RISK).** The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency has issued an information request under CERCLA § 104(e) to Cascadia regarding the Company\'s former operations at the Dalton Creek disposal facility. Although no formal enforcement action or PRP designation has been issued to date, the § 104(e) letter is a well-recognized precursor to potential enforcement activity. We estimate Cascadia\'s potential liability exposure in the range of \$1,500,000 to \$6,000,000, depending upon EPA\'s cost allocation approach and the solvency of other potentially responsible parties.

2\. **Hargrove Industrial Site Remediation (MODERATE RISK).** Cascadia is actively performing environmental remediation at the former Hargrove Industrial Site in Milwaukie, Oregon, under contract with the Oregon Department of Environmental Quality. Estimated remaining remediation costs total approximately \$4,200,000. This exposure is a contractual obligation and is covered by a site-specific environmental liability insurance policy with a \$10,000,000 policy limit, which appears adequate.

3\. **Environmental Permit Portfolio (MODERATE RISK).** Cascadia holds 23 active environmental permits across four states. Although the transaction is structured as a stock purchase, multiple state environmental regulatory programs require notification to or approval from the issuing agency upon a change in control of the permit holder. Failure to comply with these requirements could result in permit violations, enforcement actions, or permit revocation.

4\. **Government Contract Regulatory Compliance (HIGH RISK).** Cascadia is party to four active government contracts with the Oregon DEQ, Washington Department of Ecology, the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, and the Bureau of Land Management. The two federal contracts are subject to the Anti-Assignment Act and the Federal Acquisition Regulation\'s novation requirements under FAR Part 42, Subpart 42.12. Failure to obtain required novations could result in contract termination, eliminating a material revenue stream.

This memorandum provides detailed findings for each of these areas and sets forth **specific recommendations for SPA provisions** that the deal team should incorporate into its markup of the Seller\'s draft agreement. These recommendations are informed by the executed term sheet dated September 10, 2025, applicable federal and state environmental law, and industry practice for acquisitions in the environmental services sector.

Our environmental due diligence review was conducted between August 20, 2025 and October 15, 2025, following execution of the Letter of Intent between Whitmore Capital Partners LLC and Evergreen Holdings Group, Inc. on August 15, 2025. The following materials and information sources were reviewed in connection with this memorandum:

> • **Environmental Site Assessments.** Phase I and Phase II environmental site assessments for all seven of the Company\'s office and operational locations in Oregon, Washington, California, and Nevada.

> • **Environmental Permits.** Copies of all 23 active environmental remediation permits held by the Company across four states, including RCRA permits, NPDES permits, Clean Air Act emissions permits, state hazardous waste transporter permits, and state remediation contractor licenses.
> • **Compliance Records.** Environmental compliance records, agency inspection reports, and notices of violation received by the Company for the preceding five-year period (2020--2025).

> • **CERCLA Correspondence.** The EPA\'s CERCLA § 104(e) information request regarding the Dalton Creek disposal facility, dated February 12, 2025, together with the Company\'s written response thereto and all related internal correspondence and records.

> • **Remediation Contracts.** All remediation contracts, statements of work, and work plans pertaining to the Hargrove Industrial Site remediation project, including the master contract with the Oregon Department of Environmental Quality and applicable task orders.

> • **Insurance Policies.** Environmental impairment liability insurance policies issued by Northshore Specialty Insurance Co. to the Company, including the general environmental impairment liability policy (aggregate limit of \$15,000,000; per-occurrence limit of \$5,000,000) and the site-specific environmental liability insurance policy covering the Hargrove Industrial Site (policy limit of \$10,000,000).

> • **Government Contracts.** Copies of all four active government contracts between the Company and the Oregon DEQ, Washington Department of Ecology, U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, and Bureau of Land Management, including all modifications, amendments, and task orders.

> • **Professional Licenses.** Records pertaining to professional engineer (PE) licenses held by 12 employees identified as critical to maintaining permit compliance and performing permitted activities.

> • **Financial Records.** Records obtained from Winslow & Tate CPA Group, the Company\'s independent auditor, relating to environmental liability accruals reflected in the Company\'s financial statements.
**[III. Dalton Creek Disposal Facility --- CERCLA Exposure]{.underline}**

Cascadia formerly operated at the Dalton Creek disposal facility, a former hazardous waste disposal site located in Clackamas County, Oregon. The Company\'s operations at Dalton Creek involved the handling, treatment, and disposal of hazardous wastes generated by third-party industrial customers. These operations significantly predate the current management team and were conducted during a period when the Company was under different operational leadership. According to records produced during due diligence and confirmed by management interviews, Cascadia ceased all operations at the Dalton Creek disposal facility in approximately 2015.

In February 2025, the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, Region 10, issued an information request to Cascadia under Section 104(e) of the Comprehensive Environmental Response, Compensation, and Liability Act of 1980, as amended (\"CERCLA\"), 42 U.S.C. § 9604(e). The information request seeks comprehensive documentation of the Company\'s waste handling and disposal activities at the Dalton Creek facility, including waste manifests, disposal records, volume and characterization data, and operational history during the period of the Company\'s use of the site.

As of the date of this memorandum, no formal enforcement action, notice of potential responsible party (\"PRP\") designation, unilateral administrative order, or lawsuit has been filed or issued by EPA or any other party against Cascadia in connection with the Dalton Creek facility. However, the issuance of a § 104(e) information request is widely recognized as a standard precursor to potential PRP designation and subsequent enforcement activity under CERCLA. The Company\'s management confirmed that it has retained outside environmental counsel to assist with the response to the information request and to monitor developments at the site.
**[B. Estimated Liability Exposure]{.underline}**

Based on our review of the Company\'s records, the EPA information request and the Company\'s response, publicly available site information, and consultation with environmental counsel experienced in CERCLA cost allocation proceedings, we estimate Cascadia\'s potential liability exposure in connection with the Dalton Creek disposal facility to be in the range of **\$1,500,000 to \$6,000,000**. The factors underlying this range are as follows:

> • **Low End (\$1,500,000).** This estimate assumes that EPA pursues a multi-party cost allocation among all identified potentially responsible parties at the Dalton Creek site, that Cascadia\'s proportionate share of total cleanup costs is determined on the basis of the volume and toxicity of waste it disposed at the facility, and that other identified PRPs remain solvent and capable of bearing their respective shares. Under this scenario, Cascadia\'s share would represent a minority allocation consistent with its relative contribution to site contamination.

> • **High End (\$6,000,000).** This estimate reflects the possibility that EPA may designate Cascadia as a major contributor to the contamination at the site, or that one or more other PRPs may prove financially unable to satisfy their allocated shares. Under CERCLA § 107, liability is joint and several, meaning that EPA may seek recovery of the full cost of remediation from any single PRP, regardless of that party\'s proportionate contribution. If other PRPs are insolvent or unidentifiable, Cascadia\'s exposure could increase significantly. The high-end estimate also accounts for the possibility that the overall scope and cost of site remediation may exceed current projections.

It is important to note that CERCLA proceedings frequently extend over many years. Under CERCLA § 113(g)(2), the statute of limitations for a cost recovery action is six years from the date of completion of a remedial action at the site. Contribution claims under § 113(f) may extend further depending on the timing of settlement or judgment. Given that no formal remedial action has been initiated at the Dalton Creek site, it is possible that Cascadia\'s ultimate liability will not be determined for a period of years following the closing of the proposed transaction.

The Company\'s environmental impairment liability insurance with Northshore Specialty Insurance Co. (aggregate limit \$15,000,000; per-occurrence limit \$5,000,000) may provide coverage for defense costs and some portion of the Company\'s ultimate liability in connection with the Dalton Creek matter. However, coverage for legacy disposal operations is commonly subject to policy exclusions, including prior-knowledge exclusions, pollution date restrictions, and exclusions for known or disclosed conditions. We recommend that insurance counsel conduct a detailed review of the applicable policy terms to determine the extent and reliability of available coverage.
**[C. SPA Recommendations --- Dalton Creek]{.underline}**
Based on the foregoing analysis, we make the following recommendations with respect to the treatment of the Dalton Creek CERCLA exposure in the Stock Purchase Agreement:

**Recommendation 1 --- Special Indemnity.** Given the magnitude of the potential exposure (\$1,500,000 to \$6,000,000), the fact that this is a known and disclosed environmental liability arising from Seller\'s period of ownership, and the inherent uncertainty and protracted timeline of CERCLA proceedings, we **strongly recommend** that the SPA include a **Special Indemnity** obligating Seller to indemnify Buyer for all Losses arising from or related to the Dalton Creek disposal facility and the EPA\'s CERCLA § 104(e) information request, including without limitation all costs of investigation, remediation, defense, settlement, contribution, and related administrative proceedings. The Special Indemnity should be structured as follows:

> \(a\) **Survival Period.** The Special Indemnity should survive for no less than **72 months** following the closing date, in order to account for the characteristically lengthy timeline of CERCLA proceedings and the six-year statute of limitations for CERCLA cost recovery actions under § 113(g)(2). A shorter survival period would create an unacceptable risk that Buyer\'s indemnification rights expire before a formal CERCLA claim crystallizes.

> \(b\) **Exclusion from General Basket and Cap.** The Special Indemnity should **not** be subject to the general indemnification deductible basket or aggregate liability cap. The Dalton Creek matter is a known, quantifiable exposure that should be indemnified on a dollar-for-dollar basis from the first dollar of Loss. Subjecting this exposure to general basket and cap limitations would improperly shift a portion of the known risk to Buyer.

> \(c\) **Escrow Holdback.** The Special Indemnity should be supported by a dedicated portion of the **escrow holdback** maintained with Pinnacle Trust Company for a minimum period of **36 months** following closing. The escrowed amount should be sufficient to cover at least the low end of the estimated liability range (\$1,500,000), with the full Special Indemnity obligation surviving for the 72-month period regardless of the release of escrowed funds.

> \(d\) **Consistency with Term Sheet.** We note that the executed term sheet dated September 10, 2025, between Whitmore Capital Partners LLC and Evergreen Holdings Group, Inc., specifically provides for a \"Special Indemnity\" to address the Dalton Creek matter. The SPA must implement this agreed-upon commercial term. Omission of the Special Indemnity from the Seller\'s initial SPA draft would represent a departure from the agreed deal terms.

**Recommendation 2 --- Extended Survival of Environmental Representations.** Independent of and in addition to the Dalton Creek Special Indemnity, the environmental representations and warranties in the SPA should survive for a minimum of **36 months** post-closing, and ideally for the **full applicable statute of limitations** for environmental claims. We understand that seller-favorable first drafts in the middle market typically propose a 12-month survival period for representations and warranties, including environmental representations. For a company whose core business is the provision of environmental remediation and hazardous waste management services, a 12-month survival period for environmental representations would be wholly inadequate for the following reasons:
> \(a\) The Dalton Creek CERCLA exposure may not crystallize into a formal claim, enforcement action, or PRP designation for a period of years following closing, as discussed in Section III.B above.

> \(b\) Cascadia\'s active remediation projects, including the Hargrove Industrial Site project, have multi-year performance timelines during which new environmental liabilities or breaches of environmental representations may emerge.

> \(c\) Environmental liabilities in the remediation services sector routinely emerge well beyond a 12-month period due to the nature of contamination migration, delayed regulatory action, and evolving site characterization data.

> \(d\) For a company whose entire value proposition is built upon environmental compliance and permitting, the environmental representations are among the most critical representations in the agreement and should be afforded extended protection commensurate with that importance.
We recommend that the deal team take a firm position on extended survival of environmental representations during SPA negotiations.
**[IV. Hargrove Industrial Site Remediation]{.underline}**

Cascadia is currently performing active environmental remediation at the former Hargrove Industrial Site, located in Milwaukie, Oregon, under a remediation services contract with the Oregon Department of Environmental Quality (\"Oregon DEQ\"). The Hargrove project involves soil and groundwater remediation activities at the former industrial site, including excavation and off-site disposal of contaminated soil, installation and operation of a groundwater extraction and treatment system, and ongoing environmental monitoring. The Company estimates the total remaining cost to complete the remediation at approximately **\$4,200,000**, with the project expected to continue for approximately 18 to 24 months beyond the anticipated closing date. The Hargrove remediation contract is one of the Company\'s four active government contracts and represents a significant ongoing commitment of Company resources and personnel.

Cascadia carries a site-specific environmental liability insurance policy issued by **Northshore Specialty Insurance Co.** with a **\$10,000,000 policy limit** specifically covering the Hargrove Industrial Site remediation project. This policy provides coverage for remediation costs, cost overruns, and third-party claims arising from the Company\'s remediation activities at the Hargrove site. Separately, the Company\'s broader environmental impairment liability insurance with Northshore Specialty Insurance Co. carries an aggregate limit of \$15,000,000 and a per-occurrence limit of \$5,000,000. The site-specific Hargrove policy appears adequate to cover the estimated remaining \$4,200,000 remediation cost plus potential cost overruns and third-party claims, assuming no policy exclusions or coverage defenses are applicable. We recommend that the SPA include a representation that all environmental insurance policies maintained by the Company are in full force and effect, that all premiums due have been paid, and that no notice of cancellation, non-renewal, or material modification has been received. The SPA should also include a pre-closing covenant requiring the Company to maintain all such policies through and following the closing date.

We assess the Hargrove Industrial Site remediation project as a **moderate risk** item. The project is a standard remediation engagement being performed under a government contract with the Oregon DEQ. The principal risks are (i) cost overruns in excess of the current \$4,200,000 estimate, (ii) potential regulatory enforcement action if the Company fails to meet remediation milestones established in the work plan and consent order, and (iii) third-party claims arising from remediation activities. The available insurance coverage appears adequate to mitigate these risks. We note that the Oregon DEQ contract under which the Hargrove work is being performed is one of the four government contracts requiring novation or consent analysis, as discussed in Section VI below.
**[V. Environmental Permit Portfolio]{.underline}**
**[A. Overview of Permits]{.underline}**
Cascadia holds **23 active environmental remediation permits** across four states: Oregon, Washington, California, and Nevada. The permit portfolio includes the following categories:

> • **RCRA Permits.** Treatment, storage, and disposal (TSD) facility permits issued under the Resource Conservation and Recovery Act and corresponding state programs, authorizing the Company to handle, treat, store, and dispose of hazardous wastes at specified locations.

> • **Clean Water Act Discharge Permits.** National Pollutant Discharge Elimination System (NPDES) permits authorizing the Company to discharge treated water and stormwater from remediation project sites in compliance with applicable effluent limitations.
> • **Clean Air Act Emissions Permits.** Permits authorizing air emissions from remediation equipment, thermal treatment units, and related operations at Company facilities and project sites.
> • **State Hazardous Waste Transporter Permits.** Permits issued by state environmental agencies authorizing the Company to transport hazardous waste within and between states.

> • **State Remediation Contractor Licenses and Permits.** State-specific licenses and permits required to perform environmental remediation and hazardous waste management services as a licensed contractor.

All 23 permits are held in the name of Cascadia Environmental Solutions, Inc. In addition, 12 of the Company\'s employees hold professional engineer (\"PE\") licenses that are critical to maintaining permit compliance and performing permitted activities. Several of the Company\'s permits are conditioned upon the availability of a PE-licensed professional to oversee permitted operations. Loss of these PE-licensed employees, whether through attrition, termination, or failure to transfer to the post-closing entity, could jeopardize the Company\'s standing under certain permits and impair its ability to perform permitted work.

Although this transaction is structured as a **stock purchase** --- and therefore the legal entity holding the permits (Cascadia Environmental Solutions, Inc.) will not change --- many state environmental regulatory programs nonetheless require **notification to or approval from the issuing agency** upon a change in the ownership or control of the permit holder. This is a critical issue that must be addressed in the SPA. The applicable state-specific requirements include:

> • **Oregon.** Oregon DEQ regulations require notification of a change of ownership or control of a permitted facility within 30 days of such change. Certain RCRA permits issued by Oregon DEQ may require formal transfer approval prior to the change taking effect. *See* OAR Chapter 340, Division 012 and applicable permit conditions.

> • **Washington.** The Washington Department of Ecology requires prior written notification for changes in control of permitted entities. Certain permits include conditions that expressly require agency approval of ownership changes before the transfer is deemed valid. *See* WAC Chapter 173-303 and applicable permit conditions.

> • **California.** The California Department of Toxic Substances Control (\"DTSC\") and regional water quality control boards often require notification and, in certain permit categories, prior approval for changes in control of entities holding hazardous waste facility permits and waste discharge requirements. The specific requirements vary by permit type and issuing authority.

> • **Nevada.** The Nevada Division of Environmental Protection requires notification of ownership changes for certain categories of environmental permits, including hazardous waste management permits and water pollution control permits.

Even in a stock acquisition, these agencies may treat a change of the ultimate parent company --- here, the acquisition of Cascadia\'s shares by Whitmore Capital Partners LLC from Evergreen Holdings Group, Inc. --- as a \"change of ownership or control\" that triggers notification or approval requirements under the applicable permit or regulation. Failure to comply with these requirements could result in permit violations, enforcement actions, fines, or in extreme cases, permit revocation or suspension. Given that Cascadia\'s business is entirely dependent upon its ability to perform work under these permits, any disruption to the permit portfolio would be material.

We anticipate that the Seller\'s SPA draft, once circulated, will include representations that all necessary environmental permits are held by the Company and are in good standing. However, a mere representation regarding the current status of permits is insufficient to protect Buyer from the risks associated with the change-of-control process. We **strongly recommend** that the SPA include the following provisions:

> \(a\) **Pre-Closing Covenant.** A covenant requiring Seller and the Company, prior to closing, to (i) identify all environmental permits that require change-of-control notification to or approval from the issuing agency, (ii) prepare and submit all required notifications and applications for approval to the appropriate state environmental agencies, and (iii) cooperate with Buyer in providing all information reasonably requested by any such agency in connection with the change-of-control process.

> \(b\) **Post-Closing Cooperation Covenant.** A covenant obligating Seller to cooperate with Buyer following closing in completing any permit transfer, re-issuance, amendment, or notification process required by any governmental authority as a result of the change of control, including executing documents, providing historical information, and participating in agency proceedings as reasonably requested by Buyer.

> \(c\) **Survival.** These covenants should survive closing for at least **12 months**, or such longer period as may be necessary to complete all pending permit transfers and notifications, including any pending agency review or approval processes.

Affirmative covenants addressing the permit transfer and notification process are essential to protect Buyer\'s investment in a business whose value depends on the continuity of its environmental permits.
**[VI. Government Contract Regulatory Requirements]{.underline}**
**[A. Overview of Government Contracts]{.underline}**
Cascadia is party to **four active government contracts**, each of which is material to the Company\'s operations and revenue:
> 1\. **Oregon Department of Environmental Quality** --- Environmental remediation services, including the Hargrove Industrial Site remediation project discussed in Section IV above.
> 2\. **Washington Department of Ecology** --- Environmental consulting and remediation services at multiple sites within the State of Washington.
> 3\. **U.S. Army Corps of Engineers** --- Environmental assessment and remediation services at federally owned or managed properties.
> 4\. **Bureau of Land Management** --- Environmental site characterization and remediation services on federal lands managed by BLM.

These four government contracts collectively represent a material portion of Cascadia\'s annual revenue and serve as a foundation for the Company\'s ongoing business operations. Loss of any one or more of these contracts would have a material adverse effect on the Company\'s financial condition and business prospects.
**[B. Anti-Assignment Act and FAR Novation Requirements]{.underline}**

Federal government contracts are subject to the **Anti-Assignment Act, 41 U.S.C. § 6305**, which generally prohibits the transfer or assignment of government contracts without the consent of the contracting officer. While the Anti-Assignment Act has historically been interpreted to apply primarily to assignments of the contract itself (as opposed to changes in corporate ownership), the **Federal Acquisition Regulation (\"FAR\"), Part 42, Subpart 42.12**, specifically addresses changes in the contractor\'s organizational structure, including changes in ownership.

Under **FAR 42.1204**, when a contractor undergoes a change in ownership --- including when a third party acquires the stock of the contractor --- the contractor is required to submit a request for a **novation agreement** (or, in some cases, a **change-of-name agreement**) to the responsible contracting officer. A novation agreement formally recognizes the successor entity and transfers the government\'s contractual rights and obligations to the recognized successor. The key requirements under FAR 42.12 include:

> • **FAR 42.1204(a).** The contractor must submit a written request for novation to the responsible contracting officer, accompanied by supporting documentation including the acquisition agreement (or relevant portions thereof), a list of all affected contracts, and evidence of the transferee\'s technical and financial capability to perform.
> • **FAR 42.1204(e).** The contracting officer must make an affirmative determination that recognizing the successor is in the government\'s interest before executing the novation agreement.

> • **Interim Period.** Until a novation agreement is executed, the government may continue to treat the original contractor as the responsible party under the contract. Failure to obtain novation could result in the government treating the change of ownership as a breach of the contract, potentially leading to termination for default or termination for convenience.

**For the two federal contracts** --- the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers contract and the Bureau of Land Management contract --- **novation agreements will be required** under FAR 42.12 because Whitmore Capital Partners LLC, a new parent entity with no prior relationship to Cascadia, is acquiring 100% of the outstanding stock of the Company from Evergreen Holdings Group, Inc.

**For the two state contracts** --- the Oregon DEQ contract and the Washington Department of Ecology contract --- analogous state procurement regulations may impose similar notification or approval requirements for changes in corporate ownership of a government contractor. The specific requirements depend on the terms of each contract and the applicable state procurement code. These state contracts require further review of their specific provisions and the relevant Oregon and Washington procurement regulations.

**Risk Assessment.** We assess this as a **HIGH RISK** item. Failure to obtain required novation agreements or government consents could result in **contract termination**, which would eliminate a material revenue stream, potentially trigger cross-default provisions under the Company\'s other contracts or financing arrangements, and materially impair the value of Buyer\'s investment. The novation process is not merely administrative --- contracting officers have discretion to deny novation if they determine that the successor entity does not have the capability or resources to perform, or if recognition is not in the government\'s interest.
**[C. SPA Recommendations --- Government Contracts]{.underline}**

**Recommendation 1 --- Pre-Closing Covenant.** The SPA should include a specific covenant requiring Seller and the Company to (a) promptly notify each government contracting officer (federal and state) of the contemplated transaction, (b) submit all required novation request packages under FAR 42.12 for the two federal contracts and all analogous submissions required under state procurement regulations for the two state contracts, and (c) use commercially reasonable efforts to obtain all required novation agreements, recognition agreements, or government consents prior to closing.

**Recommendation 2 --- Closing Condition or Specific Covenant.** The deal team should carefully consider whether to make completion of the government contract novation process a **condition to closing** or a **pre-closing best-efforts covenant with a post-closing cooperation tail**. Given that the FAR novation process can take 60 to 120 days or longer, requiring full novation completion as a hard closing condition could delay closing beyond the expected mid-January 2026 timeline or the February 28, 2026 outside date set forth in the term sheet. We recommend the following balanced approach:
> \(a\) Require that all novation requests and government notifications have been **submitted** to all relevant contracting officers prior to closing.

> \(b\) Require that no government contracting officer has **denied** a novation request or indicated an intent to terminate, suspend, or materially modify any government contract as a result of the contemplated transaction.

> \(c\) Include a **post-closing cooperation covenant** requiring Seller to continue cooperating in the novation process following closing, including executing documents, providing information, and participating in meetings with contracting officers as reasonably requested by Buyer.

**Recommendation 3 --- Representations.** The SPA should include specific representations that (a) Seller has provided complete and accurate copies of all government contracts, including all modifications, amendments, and task orders, (b) the Company is in material compliance with all terms of such government contracts, (c) no government contract is the subject of any pending or threatened termination, suspension, or debarment proceeding, and (d) to Seller\'s Knowledge, no contracting officer has indicated any intent to terminate, not renew, or materially modify any such contract.

**Recommendation 4 --- Risk Allocation.** If any government contract is terminated as a result of the change of ownership and the failure to obtain the required novation agreement or government consent, the resulting Losses --- including lost revenue, contract penalties, and consequential damages --- should be allocated to Seller through the indemnification provisions of the SPA.

We note that the Seller\'s SPA draft should be carefully reviewed to determine whether the conditions-to-closing article addresses government contract consents separately from general third-party consents. It is common in seller-favorable first drafts to group government contract consents with general commercial consents --- this approach is insufficient given the unique federal regulatory framework applicable to government contracts and the heightened risk of contract termination. Government contract novation should be treated as a distinct and specifically addressed closing requirement.
**[VII. Environmental Insurance Summary]{.underline}**
Cascadia maintains the following environmental insurance program, both policies issued by Northshore Specialty Insurance Co.:

**Environmental Impairment Liability (\"EIL\") Insurance.** The Company\'s general EIL policy provides coverage for third-party claims arising from pollution conditions associated with the Company\'s operations. The policy carries an aggregate limit of \$15,000,000 and a per-occurrence limit of \$5,000,000. The policy covers defense costs, remediation costs, and bodily injury and property damage claims resulting from pollution events. The EIL policy is the Company\'s primary environmental insurance coverage and applies across all of the Company\'s operations and locations.

**Hargrove Site-Specific Policy.** In addition to the general EIL policy, the Company maintains a project-specific environmental liability policy covering the Hargrove Industrial Site remediation project. This policy carries a \$10,000,000 policy limit and provides coverage for remediation costs, cost overruns, and third-party claims arising specifically from the Company\'s remediation activities at the Hargrove site.

As discussed in Section III.B above, coverage for the Dalton Creek matter under the general EIL policy is uncertain. Legacy disposal operations conducted at the Dalton Creek facility may be subject to policy exclusions, including prior-knowledge exclusions, pollution date restrictions, and exclusions for known or previously disclosed environmental conditions. We recommend that insurance counsel be engaged to conduct a detailed review of the EIL policy terms and conditions to determine the extent of available coverage for the Dalton Creek CERCLA exposure and to assess the risk of coverage denial.

We recommend that the SPA include (a) a representation that all environmental insurance policies maintained by the Company are in full force and effect, that all premiums due thereunder have been paid in full, and that no notice of cancellation, non-renewal, or material modification has been received, and (b) a pre-closing covenant requiring the Company to maintain all such policies in full force and effect through and following closing.

The results of this review may affect the sizing of the Special Indemnity escrow.

> • **Environmental Permit Representations.** Confirm that the Seller\'s environmental representations in the SPA specifically cover all 23 active environmental permits, including a representation that each permit is valid, in good standing, and not subject to any pending or threatened revocation, suspension, or modification.

> • **Government Contract Novation as Closing Condition.** Whether completion of the government contract novation process should be a hard closing condition versus a best-efforts pre-closing covenant with a post-closing tail. A separate escrow would provide clearer protection for Buyer but may be resisted by Seller as adding administrative complexity.

The environmental due diligence conducted by the Environmental Practice Group has identified material environmental risks associated with the acquisition of Cascadia Environmental Solutions, Inc. that must be addressed through specific provisions in the Stock Purchase Agreement. This **STOCK PURCHASE AGREEMENT** (this \"Agreement\") is made and entered into as of \[●\], 2025, by and among **Evergreen Holdings Group, Inc.**, a Delaware corporation (\"Seller\"), **Whitmore Capital Partners LLC**, a Delaware limited liability company (\"Buyer\"), and, solely for the purposes of Sections 4.01 through 4.21, Section 6.01, Section 6.02, and Section 6.03, **Cascadia Environmental Solutions, Inc.**, an Oregon corporation (the \"Company\"). **C.** The Company is engaged in the business of environmental remediation, hazardous waste management, and environmental consulting services, and is headquartered in Tualatin, Oregon, with operations in the states of Oregon, Washington, California, and Nevada.

**D.** Concurrently with the execution and delivery of this Agreement, the Parties are entering into, or will enter into, certain ancillary agreements as further described herein, including the Escrow Agreement and the other Transaction Documents.

**NOW, THEREFORE**, in consideration of the foregoing recitals and the mutual covenants, representations, warranties, and agreements contained herein, and for other good and valuable consideration, the receipt and sufficiency of which are hereby acknowledged, the Parties agree as follows:
**Section 1.01 Defined Terms**

\"**Action**\" means any claim, action, suit, proceeding, arbitration, mediation, investigation, inquiry, hearing, charge, complaint, demand, or notice by or before any Governmental Authority or arbitration tribunal.

\"**Adjusted EBITDA**\" means, with respect to any period, the net income of the Company for such period, determined in accordance with GAAP applied consistently with the Company\'s past practice, plus (a) interest expense, (b) income tax expense, and (c) depreciation and amortization expense, in each case to the extent deducted in computing net income, and further adjusted to exclude (i) non-recurring transaction costs incurred in connection with the transactions contemplated by this Agreement, (ii) any purchase-price accounting adjustments arising from the consummation of the transactions contemplated hereby, (iii) any extraordinary or non-recurring items, and (iv) any management fees, monitoring fees, or similar fees charged by Buyer or any of its Affiliates to the Company, in each case as determined in accordance with GAAP applied consistently with the Company\'s past practice. The detailed calculation methodology for Adjusted EBITDA is set forth on Exhibit D.

\"**Affiliate**\" means, with respect to any Person, any other Person that directly or indirectly controls, is controlled by, or is under common control with, such Person. For purposes of this definition, \"control\" (including the terms \"controlled by\" and \"under common control with\") means the possession, directly or indirectly, of the power to direct or cause the direction of the management and policies of a Person, whether through the ownership of voting securities, by contract, or otherwise.

\"**Basket Amount**\" means Two Million One Hundred Fifty Thousand Dollars (\$2,150,000), which is equal to one percent (1%) of the Base Enterprise Value. The Basket Amount shall operate as a true deductible (and not as a \"tipping\" or \"first-dollar\" basket).
\"**Buyer Indemnitees**\" has the meaning set forth in Section 9.02.
\"**Closing**\" has the meaning set forth in Section 2.07.
\"**Closing Date**\" has the meaning set forth in Section 2.07.
\"**Closing Payment**\" has the meaning set forth in Section 2.03(b).
\"**Closing Statement**\" has the meaning set forth in Section 2.04(a).
\"**Company Material Contracts**\" has the meaning set forth in Section 4.13.
\"**Earnout Payment**\" has the meaning set forth in Section 2.05(a).
\"**Earnout Period**\" means the twelve (12) month period commencing on January 1, 2026 and ending on December 31, 2026.

\"**Employee Benefit Plan**\" means each \"employee benefit plan\" (as defined in Section 3(3) of ERISA), and each other plan, program, policy, agreement, or arrangement providing compensation, severance, retention, change of control, deferred compensation, equity-based compensation, fringe benefits, insurance (including self-insured arrangements), medical, hospital, dental, vision, prescription drug, disability, supplemental unemployment benefits, profit-sharing, pension, retirement benefits, or post-employment or post-retirement benefits, in each case that is sponsored, maintained, contributed to, or required to be contributed to by the Company for the benefit of any current or former employee, officer, director, consultant, or independent contractor of the Company, or with respect to which the Company has or could have any liability.

\"**Environmental Laws**\" means all federal, state, and local Laws, and all judicial and administrative orders and decrees, relating to pollution, the protection of the environment or natural resources, or human health and safety (as it relates to exposure to Hazardous Substances), including the Comprehensive Environmental Response, Compensation, and Liability Act of 1980, as amended (\"CERCLA\"), the Resource Conservation and Recovery Act, as amended (\"RCRA\"), the Clean Air Act, as amended, the Federal Water Pollution Control Act (the \"Clean Water Act\"), as amended, the Toxic Substances Control Act (\"TSCA\"), as amended, the Hazardous Materials Transportation Act, as amended, the Oil Pollution Act of 1990, as amended, the Safe Drinking Water Act, as amended, and any and all analogues or equivalents of the foregoing under any applicable state or local Law, including the Oregon Environmental Cleanup Law (ORS 465.200 et seq.), the Washington Model Toxics Control Act (RCW 70A.305), the California Health and Safety Code (Division 20), and the Nevada Revised Statutes (Chapter 459).

**Section 2.02 Purchase Price**

The aggregate purchase price for the Shares (the \"Purchase Price\") shall be an amount equal to (a) the Base Enterprise Value (\$215,000,000), *plus* (b) the amount, if any, by which the Estimated Closing NWC exceeds the Target NWC, *minus* (c) the amount, if any, by which the Target NWC exceeds the Estimated Closing NWC, *minus* (d) the Estimated Closing Indebtedness, *minus* (e) the Estimated Transaction Expenses. For illustrative purposes only, based on preliminary estimates, the Purchase Price would be calculated as follows: \$215,000,000 + \$18,200,000 (Estimated Closing NWC at Target) -- \$42,300,000 (Estimated Closing Indebtedness) -- \$3,900,000 (Estimated Transaction Expenses) = \$187,000,000. The Purchase Price shall be subject to adjustment as provided in Sections 2.03 and 2.04. The Purchase Price does not include any Earnout Payment that may become payable pursuant to Section 2.05, which shall be in addition to the Purchase Price.
**Section 2.03 Closing Payment and Estimates**

**(a)** *Pre-Closing Estimate.* Not later than three (3) Business Days prior to the Closing Date, Seller shall prepare and deliver to Buyer a written statement (the \"Estimated Closing Statement\") setting forth Seller\'s good-faith estimates of: (i) the Closing NWC (the \"Estimated Closing NWC\"), (ii) the Closing Indebtedness (the \"Estimated Closing Indebtedness\"), and (iii) the Transaction Expenses (the \"Estimated Transaction Expenses\"), together with reasonable supporting documentation, schedules, and work papers used in the preparation thereof. The Estimated Closing Statement shall be prepared in accordance with the Accounting Principles and shall include a calculation of the estimated Purchase Price based on such estimates. Seller shall provide Buyer with reasonable access to the books and records of the Company and the work papers of the Company\'s accountants as Buyer may reasonably request to verify the Estimated Closing Statement. If Buyer delivers written notice of any objections to the Estimated Closing Statement within two (2) Business Days after receipt thereof, the Parties shall negotiate in good faith to resolve such objections prior to the Closing Date; *provided* that the failure of the Parties to resolve any such objections shall not delay the Closing, and the Estimated Closing Statement, as adjusted by mutual agreement of the Parties (or, absent such agreement, as originally delivered by Seller), shall be used for purposes of calculating the Closing Payment, subject to the post-Closing adjustment procedures set forth in Section 2.04.

**(b)** *Closing Payment.* At the Closing, Buyer shall pay to Seller an aggregate amount in cash (the \"Closing Payment\") equal to (i) the Purchase Price (calculated using the estimates set forth in the Estimated Closing Statement), *minus* (ii) the Escrow Amount (\$16,125,000). The Closing Payment shall be made by wire transfer of immediately available funds to one or more bank accounts designated in writing by Seller to Buyer no later than two (2) Business Days prior to the Closing Date.

**(c)** *Escrow Deposit.* At the Closing, Buyer shall deposit the Escrow Amount, in cash, by wire transfer of immediately available funds, with the Escrow Agent in accordance with the terms of the Escrow Agreement. **Section 2.05 Earnout**

**(a)** *Maximum Earnout Payment.* If the Company\'s Adjusted EBITDA for the Earnout Period (the twelve (12) month period ending December 31, 2026) equals or exceeds Thirty-Eight Million Dollars (\$38,000,000), Buyer shall pay to Seller an amount equal to Twenty-Five Million Dollars (\$25,000,000) (the \"Maximum Earnout Payment\").

**(b)** *Pro-Rata Earnout.* If the Company\'s Adjusted EBITDA for the Earnout Period is at least Thirty-Two Million Dollars (\$32,000,000) but less than Thirty-Eight Million Dollars (\$38,000,000), Buyer shall pay to Seller an amount (the \"Earnout Payment\") equal to: (\$25,000,000 ÷ (\$38,000,000 -- \$32,000,000)) × (Actual Adjusted EBITDA -- \$32,000,000). For the avoidance of doubt, this formula results in a linear interpolation, such that the Earnout Payment increases by approximately Four Million One Hundred Sixty-Six Thousand Six Hundred Sixty-Seven Dollars (\$4,166,667) for each One Million Dollars (\$1,000,000) of Adjusted EBITDA in excess of \$32,000,000. If the Company\'s Adjusted EBITDA for the Earnout Period is less than \$32,000,000, no Earnout Payment shall be due or payable.

**(c)** *Earnout Calculation and Dispute Resolution.* Within sixty (60) days after the end of the Earnout Period, Buyer shall prepare and deliver to Seller a written statement (the \"Earnout Statement\") setting forth Buyer\'s good-faith calculation of Adjusted EBITDA for the Earnout Period, together with reasonable supporting documentation. Seller shall have thirty (30) days to review the Earnout Statement and deliver any objections thereto. The dispute resolution procedures set forth in Section 2.04(b) and Section 2.04(c) shall apply *mutatis mutandis* to any dispute with respect to the Earnout Statement.

**(d)** *Operation of the Business During the Earnout Period.* From and after the Closing Date through the end of the Earnout Period, Buyer shall, and shall cause the Company to, operate the business of the Company in a manner consistent with past practice and in good faith to maximize the Earnout Payment. Without limiting the foregoing, Buyer shall not, and shall cause the Company not to, take any action that would reasonably be expected to reduce the Adjusted EBITDA of the Company below the levels that would otherwise have been achieved. In furtherance of the foregoing, during the Earnout Period, Buyer shall cause the Company to maintain substantially the same level of personnel, equipment, and other resources as in effect immediately prior to the Closing Date and shall not divert or redirect any contracts, customers, revenues, or business opportunities of the Company to Buyer or any of its Affiliates. Notwithstanding the foregoing, Buyer acknowledges and agrees that Seller shall have no obligation to contribute resources, personnel, or funds to the Company during the Earnout Period, and the obligations set forth in this Section 2.05(d) are solely obligations of Buyer.

**(e)** *Payment of Earnout.* Any Earnout Payment determined to be payable pursuant to this Section 2.05 shall be paid by Buyer to Seller within ten (10) Business Days after the final determination of Adjusted EBITDA for the Earnout Period (whether by agreement of the Parties, expiration of the review period without objection, or determination of the Independent Accountant), by wire transfer of immediately available funds to the account designated by Seller. For U.S. federal income tax purposes, the Parties agree to treat any Earnout Payment as an adjustment to the Purchase Price.
